articles.title: Better Sleep: Simple Habits for More Rested Nights
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Good sleep helps your body repair itself, keeps your mood steady and helps you learn and remember. Many people sleep too little without noticing, so small changes can make a big difference.

## How much sleep do you need?

Health experts such as the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) give these general guides:

- Adults: 7 hours or more each night
- Teenagers (13 to 17 years): 8 to 10 hours
- Children aged 6 to 12: 9 to 12 hours
- Young children need even more, often including naps

Everyone is a little different. A good sign is that you wake up feeling rested and do not feel very sleepy during the day.

## Build a steady routine

Your body has an inner clock, sometimes called the circadian rhythm. It works best when you go to bed and wake up at about the same time every day, including weekends.

1. Choose a wake-up time you can keep every day.
2. Count back 7 to 9 hours to find your bedtime.
3. Start to relax about 30 minutes before that time.
4. Get some daylight in the morning. Light helps set your inner clock.

## Make your bedroom sleep-friendly

- Keep the room quiet, dark and cool.
- Put phones, tablets and laptops away at least 30 minutes before bed. Screens keep the brain alert.
- Use your bed for sleep, not for work or long hours of scrolling.

What you eat and drink matters too. Caffeine is a substance that keeps you awake. It is found in coffee, tea, energy drinks and many soft drinks. Its effect can last for hours, so try to avoid it in the afternoon and evening. Large, heavy meals late at night can also make sleep harder. Regular exercise during the day helps many people fall asleep faster, but very hard exercise right before bed may not.

## If you cannot sleep

If you are lying awake for a long time, get up, go to a calm place with low light, and do something quiet, like reading a paper book. Go back to bed when you feel sleepy. Worrying about sleep often makes it worse.

See a doctor if poor sleep lasts for several weeks, if you feel very tired every day, or if someone tells you that you snore loudly and seem to stop breathing in your sleep. These can be signs of a sleep problem that can be treated.

## Key points

- Most adults need 7 hours of sleep or more each night.
- Going to bed and waking up at the same time every day helps your inner clock.
- Put screens away at least 30 minutes before bed.
- Avoid caffeine in the afternoon and evening.
- See a doctor if sleep problems last for weeks.

Further reading: CDC, NHS, Mayo Clinic

quiz.explain: The article says most adults need 7 hours or more.

options: Right as you close your eyes
quiz.explain: Screens keep the brain alert, so put them away at least 30 minutes before bed.

quiz.q: What should you do if you lie awake for a long time?
options: Get up and do something quiet until you feel sleepy
quiz.explain: The article suggests getting up and doing something calm until you feel sleepy.

articles.title: Staying Safe in the Heat: Water, Shade and Warning Signs
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
In hot countries, summer heat can make anyone ill, not only older people or athletes. Knowing how to stay cool, and how to spot heat exhaustion early, can protect you and your family.

## How to stay cool and hydrated

Hydration means having enough water in your body. In hot weather you lose water through sweat, often faster than you notice.

- Drink water regularly through the day. Do not wait until you feel very thirsty.
- Check your urine. Pale yellow usually means you are drinking enough. Dark yellow can be a sign you need more water.
- Limit very sugary drinks and energy drinks.
- Stay in the shade or indoors during the hottest part of the day, usually around midday and the early afternoon.
- Wear light, loose clothing and a hat outside.
- Never leave a child or a pet in a parked car, even for a few minutes. Cars heat up very quickly.

## What is heat exhaustion?

Heat exhaustion happens when the body gets too hot and loses too much water and salt. Signs include:

- Tiredness, dizziness or a headache
- Feeling sick or vomiting
- Heavy sweating and pale, clammy (cool and damp) skin
- Cramps in the arms, legs or stomach
- Very strong thirst and a high temperature

## What to do

The UK's National Health Service (NHS) gives these steps:

1. Move the person to a cool place.
2. Remove extra clothing.
3. Give plenty of water. An oral rehydration drink (a powder mixed with water that replaces salts) or a sports drink can also help.
4. Cool their skin with cool water, by fanning, or with cold packs wrapped in cloth under the armpits or on the neck.

Stay with them. They should start to feel better within about 30 minutes.

## When it becomes an emergency

Heatstroke is more serious than heat exhaustion. The body can no longer cool itself. Call your local emergency number if the person:

- Still feels unwell after 30 minutes of rest, cooling and fluids
- Has hot skin that is not sweating
- Is confused, cannot walk properly, has a seizure (fit) or faints
- Has a very fast heartbeat or fast breathing

While you wait, keep cooling them with wet cloths and fanning.

## Key points

- Drink water regularly in hot weather; pale urine is a good sign.
- Avoid the midday sun and never leave anyone in a parked car.
- Heat exhaustion causes dizziness, headache, heavy sweating and cramps.
- Cool the person down and give fluids; they should improve within 30 minutes.
- Hot, dry skin or confusion can mean heatstroke: call for emergency help.

Further reading: NHS, CDC, WHO

quiz.explain: The article says pale yellow usually means you are drinking enough.

quiz.q: Within about how long should someone with heat exhaustion start to feel better after cooling and drinking?
quiz.explain: The NHS says they should start to improve within about 30 minutes.

quiz.q: Which sign suggests heatstroke and needs emergency help?
options: Hot skin that is not sweating and confusion
quiz.explain: Hot, dry skin and confusion are signs of heatstroke, an emergency.

articles.title: Blood Pressure Explained: The Silent Risk and How to Lower It
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
High blood pressure often has no symptoms, so many people have it without knowing. Over time it can damage the heart, brain and kidneys, but simple checks and daily habits can help.

## What is blood pressure?

Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of your blood vessels. It is written as two numbers, for example 120/80.

- The top number (systolic) is the pressure when your heart beats.
- The bottom number (diastolic) is the pressure when your heart rests between beats.

The World Health Organization (WHO) says high blood pressure, also called hypertension, is usually diagnosed when readings on two different days are 140/90 or higher. Your doctor will explain what your own numbers mean.

## Why it matters

The WHO estimates that about 1.4 billion adults aged 30 to 79 have high blood pressure, and about 44% of them do not know it. Untreated, it raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease. This is why it is often called a "silent" risk.

## Get it checked

- Have your blood pressure measured at a clinic or pharmacy, even if you feel well.
- Home blood pressure monitors are also available. Sit quietly for a few minutes before measuring.
- Ask a health worker how often you should check, especially if high blood pressure runs in your family.

## Daily habits that help

1. Eat less salt. The WHO advises adults to eat less than 5 grams of salt a day, which is just under one teaspoon. Much salt is hidden in bread, processed meat, snacks, sauces and stock cubes, so read food labels.
2. Eat more vegetables and fruit.
3. Move more. Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, such as brisk walking. That is about 30 minutes on 5 days.
4. Keep a healthy weight.
5. Do not smoke or use tobacco.
6. Find ways to manage stress and sleep well.

If a doctor prescribes medicine for blood pressure, take it as directed. Do not stop it on your own, even if you feel fine.

See a doctor urgently if you have a very high reading together with chest pain, a severe headache, trouble speaking, or weakness on one side of the body.

## Key points

- Blood pressure is written as two numbers, such as 120/80.
- High blood pressure often has no symptoms, so get it checked.
- WHO advises less than 5 grams of salt a day.
- Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week.
- Take prescribed medicine as directed and do not stop it on your own.

Further reading: WHO, NHS, Mayo Clinic

quiz.q: Why is high blood pressure called a silent risk?
quiz.explain: Many people have high blood pressure without any symptoms.

quiz.q: How much salt does the WHO advise adults to eat at most each day?
quiz.explain: WHO advises less than 5 grams of salt a day, just under a teaspoon.

quiz.q: How much moderate activity per week does the article suggest?
quiz.explain: The article recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.

articles.title: Preventing Type 2 Diabetes: Small Changes, Big Results
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Type 2 diabetes is one of the most common long-term illnesses in the world, and the Middle East and North Africa region has some of the highest rates. The good news is that it can often be prevented or delayed with everyday habits.

## What is type 2 diabetes?

When you eat, your body turns food into sugar (glucose) for energy. A hormone called insulin helps that sugar move from your blood into your cells. In type 2 diabetes, the body does not use insulin well, so sugar builds up in the blood. Over many years, high blood sugar can damage the eyes, kidneys, nerves, heart and feet.

Before type 2 diabetes, many people have prediabetes. This means blood sugar is higher than normal but not yet high enough to be diabetes. It usually has no signs, so most people with it do not know.

## Who is at higher risk?

- People with a parent, brother or sister with type 2 diabetes
- People over about 45 years old
- People who are overweight, especially around the waist
- People who are not physically active
- Women who had diabetes during pregnancy
- People with high blood pressure

## Steps that lower your risk

Large studies, such as the US Diabetes Prevention Program, found that people with prediabetes who lost a modest amount of weight and became more active were much less likely to develop type 2 diabetes. The CDC says lifestyle programs like this can cut the risk about in half.

1. Move more. Aim for about 150 minutes of activity a week, such as walking 30 minutes on 5 days. In hot weather, walk early in the morning, in the evening, or in a mall.
2. If you are overweight, losing even 5 to 7% of your body weight can help. For someone who weighs 90 kg, that is about 4.5 to 6 kg.
3. Cut down on sugary drinks, including juices, sweetened tea and soft drinks. Drink water instead.
4. Choose whole grains, vegetables, beans and lentils more often than white bread, white rice and sweets.
5. Enjoy dates and traditional sweets in small portions.

## Get tested

A simple blood test can show if you have prediabetes or diabetes. Ask your doctor about testing, especially if you have any of the risk factors above.

See a doctor if you notice strong thirst, passing urine often, tiredness, blurred vision, or cuts that heal slowly. These can be signs of diabetes.

## Key points

- In type 2 diabetes, the body does not use insulin well and blood sugar rises.
- Prediabetes usually has no signs, so a blood test is important.
- Losing 5 to 7% of body weight and staying active can greatly lower risk.
- Swap sugary drinks for water.
- See a doctor if you have strong thirst, frequent urination or blurred vision.

Further reading: CDC, WHO, International Diabetes Federation, NIDDK

quiz.q: What does the hormone insulin do?
options: Helps sugar move from the blood into cells
quiz.explain: Insulin helps sugar move from the blood into the body's cells.

quiz.q: Why is a blood test important for prediabetes?
quiz.explain: Prediabetes usually has no signs, so most people do not know they have it.

quiz.q: How much weight loss can help lower risk for someone who is overweight?
quiz.explain: The article says losing even 5 to 7% of body weight can help.

articles.title: Screens and Your Eyes: How to Prevent Tired, Dry Eyes
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Many of us look at phones, computers and TVs for hours every day. This can leave your eyes tired, dry or blurry. The good news is that a few simple habits can help a lot.

## What is digital eye strain?

Digital eye strain means discomfort after long screen use. Common signs are:

- Dry, tired or sore eyes
- Blurred vision
- Headaches
- Neck and shoulder pain

According to the American Academy of Ophthalmology (eye doctors), screens do not cause permanent damage to your eyes. The discomfort is usually temporary and gets better with rest.

Why does it happen? Normally we blink about 15 times a minute. When we look at a screen, we blink much less, often only 5 to 7 times a minute. Fewer blinks mean the eyes dry out. Focusing on something close for a long time also tires the eye muscles.

## Simple habits that help

1. Follow the 20-20-20 rule. Every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds. This lets your eye muscles relax.
2. Blink on purpose. A small note on your screen can remind you.
3. Keep the screen about an arm's length away, a little below eye level.
4. Match the screen brightness to the room. A screen much brighter than the room makes your eyes work harder.
5. Reduce glare from windows and lamps.
6. If your eyes feel dry, lubricating eye drops (sometimes called artificial tears) from a pharmacy may help.

## Children and screens

Children's eyes are still growing. Research suggests that spending time outdoors in daylight may help lower the chance that children become short-sighted. Short-sighted (myopia) means far things look blurry. Encourage children to take screen breaks and to play outside every day, using shade and hats in hot weather.

## Get your eyes checked

Sometimes eye strain happens because you need glasses or your glasses are out of date. Have regular eye tests, and take children for eye checks too.

See an eye doctor if you have eye pain, sudden changes in vision, flashes of light, or problems that do not improve with rest.

## Key points

- Screens can cause tired, dry eyes, but not permanent damage.
- We blink much less when looking at screens.
- Use the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
- Keep screens an arm's length away and match brightness to the room.
- Time outdoors and regular eye tests are good for children's eyes.

Further reading: American Academy of Ophthalmology, NHS, Cleveland Clinic

quiz.q: What is the 20-20-20 rule?
options: Use screens for only 20 minutes a day
Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds
quiz.explain: Every 20 minutes, look about 20 feet away for 20 seconds.

quiz.q: Why do eyes get dry when using screens?
quiz.explain: We blink much less often when looking at screens.

quiz.q: According to eye doctors, do screens cause permanent eye damage?
options: No, the discomfort is usually temporary
quiz.explain: The article says screens do not cause permanent damage; discomfort is usually temporary.

articles.title: Managing Stress and Anxiety: Calm Techniques That Work
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Everyone feels stress sometimes, from exams, work, money or family life. A little stress is normal, but too much for too long can affect your sleep, mood and health. Learning a few calming skills can help you feel more in control.

## Stress and anxiety: what is the difference?

Stress is how your body and mind react to pressure. Your heart may beat faster and your muscles may tighten. Anxiety is a feeling of worry or fear, often about things that might happen. Both are common and are nothing to be ashamed of.

Signs can include:

- Trouble sleeping or feeling tired
- Headaches or a tight chest
- Feeling irritable (easily annoyed)
- Finding it hard to concentrate
- Eating much more or much less than usual

## A simple breathing exercise

The UK's National Health Service (NHS) suggests this exercise. You can do it anywhere.

1. Sit or stand comfortably and loosen tight clothing.
2. Breathe in gently through your nose while counting from 1 to 5. Let the breath go deep into your belly.
3. Breathe out gently through your mouth while counting from 1 to 5.
4. Keep going for at least 5 minutes.

It may feel strange at first. Practising every day makes it easier to use when you feel stressed.

## Everyday habits that help

- Move your body. A walk, even a short one, can lift your mood.
- Keep a regular sleep routine.
- Talk to someone you trust, such as a friend, family member, teacher or religious leader.
- Break big problems into small steps and write a short to-do list.
- Take breaks from news and social media.
- Make time for things you enjoy, and for prayer or quiet reflection if that is part of your life.
- Limit caffeine, which can make anxiety feel worse.

## When to get help

Getting help is a sign of strength. Talk to a doctor or mental health professional if:

- Stress or worry lasts for weeks and does not improve
- It stops you from working, studying or enjoying life
- You have panic attacks (sudden waves of strong fear with a racing heart)
- You feel hopeless

If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, contact your local emergency number or a crisis helpline straight away, or tell someone near you.

## Key points

- Stress and anxiety are common and nothing to be ashamed of.
- Slow breathing in and out for a count of 5 can help you calm down.
- Exercise, sleep and talking to someone you trust all help.
- Take breaks from news and social media.
- Seek professional help if worry lasts for weeks or stops you living normally.

Further reading: NHS, WHO, Mayo Clinic

quiz.q: In the NHS breathing exercise, how long should you count for each breath in?
quiz.explain: Breathe in gently while counting from 1 to 5.

quiz.q: Which habit can make anxiety feel worse?
quiz.explain: The article says caffeine can make anxiety feel worse.

quiz.q: When should you talk to a doctor about stress?
options: Only if you have a fever
If it lasts for weeks or stops you living normally
quiz.explain: Seek help if stress lasts for weeks or affects work, study or daily life.

articles.title: First Aid Basics: Burns, Choking and Bleeding
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Accidents happen at home, at school and on the road. Knowing a few first aid steps can protect someone until professional help arrives. This is general guidance; a first aid course is the best way to learn.

## Burns and scalds

A scald is a burn from hot liquid or steam. The UK's National Health Service (NHS) advises:

1. Stop the burning. Move away from the heat source.
2. Cool the burn under cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice.
3. Remove clothing or jewellery near the burn, but do not pull off anything stuck to the skin.
4. Cover the burn loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag.

Do not put butter, oil, toothpaste or creams on a burn, and do not pop blisters. Get emergency help if the burn is large or deep, is on the face, hands, feet or private parts, or was caused by chemicals or electricity. Burns on babies and young children should always be checked by a health worker.

## Choking

If an adult or older child is choking but can still cough, encourage them to keep coughing. If they cannot cough, speak or breathe:

1. Give up to 5 back blows. Help them lean forward and hit firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand (the part between your palm and wrist).
2. If that does not work, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts. Stand behind them, put a fist just above their belly button, hold it with your other hand, and pull sharply inwards and upwards.
3. If the blockage is still there, call your local emergency number and keep repeating back blows and abdominal thrusts until help arrives.

Do not give abdominal thrusts to babies under 1 year old or to pregnant women. Babies need a different method, which is taught on first aid courses. If the person becomes unconscious, call for help and start CPR (chest compressions) if you have been trained.

## Heavy bleeding

1. Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or bandage.
2. Keep pressing. If blood soaks through, add another cloth on top. Do not remove the first one.
3. If possible, raise the injured part above the level of the heart.
4. Call your local emergency number for heavy bleeding that does not stop.

If you can, wear gloves or use a plastic bag over your hands to protect yourself.

## Be prepared

- Save your local emergency number in your phone.
- Keep a simple first aid kit at home and in the car.
- Consider a first aid course from a recognised group such as the Red Cross or Red Crescent.

## Key points

- Cool a burn under running water for 20 minutes; no butter, ice or creams.
- For choking, give up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts.
- Never give abdominal thrusts to babies under 1 or to pregnant women.
- For bleeding, press firmly on the wound and keep pressing.
- A first aid course is the best way to be ready.

Further reading: NHS, British Red Cross, St John Ambulance, Mayo Clinic

quiz.q: How long should you cool a burn under running water?
options: Do not use water; use butter
quiz.explain: The NHS advises cooling a burn under running water for 20 minutes.

quiz.q: What is the first step for a choking adult who cannot cough or breathe?
quiz.explain: Start with up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades.

quiz.q: Who should NOT be given abdominal thrusts?
quiz.explain: Abdominal thrusts are not given to babies under 1 year old or pregnant women.

articles.title: Staying Healthy While Fasting: Tips for Ramadan and Beyond
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Millions of people fast each year, especially during Ramadan, when Muslims do not eat or drink from dawn to sunset. With good planning, most healthy adults can fast safely and keep their energy up.

## Do not skip suhoor

Suhoor is the meal before dawn. Skipping it makes the fasting day longer and makes tiredness and dehydration more likely. Dehydration means your body does not have enough water.

Good suhoor choices release energy slowly:

- Oats, whole-grain bread or brown rice
- Eggs, beans, lentils, yoghurt or cheese
- Fruit and vegetables, which also contain water
- Plenty of water

Try to limit very salty foods at suhoor, such as pickles and salty cheese, because salt makes you thirsty.

## Break the fast gently

At iftar, many people start with water and a few dates, following tradition. Dates give quick natural sugar. Then eat a balanced meal with vegetables, some protein (meat, fish, chicken, beans) and starchy foods. Avoid eating very large amounts at once. Fried foods and rich sweets are fine sometimes, but too much can cause indigestion and weight gain.

## Drink well between sunset and dawn

- Spread your water through the evening and night instead of drinking a lot at once.
- Soups, fruit such as watermelon, and vegetables add fluid.
- Limit caffeine and very sugary drinks.
- In hot weather, stay in the shade and avoid hard physical work during the hottest hours.

Mild headaches and tiredness are common, especially in the first days. Light activity, such as a short walk after iftar, can help you feel better.

## Fasting with a health condition

Islam allows people who are ill, pregnant, breastfeeding, elderly or travelling not to fast, and there are other ways to take part. If you have a long-term condition such as diabetes, heart disease or kidney disease, or you take regular medicine, speak to your doctor before you fast. People with diabetes can be at risk of very low or very high blood sugar and dehydration. A doctor may need to change the timing of medicines. Do not change your medicine on your own.

Stop fasting and get medical help if you feel faint or confused, are very weak, have chest pain, or show signs of severe dehydration, such as very dark urine or not passing urine.

## Key points

- Do not skip suhoor; choose slow-release foods and water.
- Break the fast gently with water and a few dates, then a balanced meal.
- Spread drinks through the evening and limit salt and caffeine.
- People with diabetes or other conditions should talk to a doctor before fasting.
- Stop fasting and get help if you feel faint, confused or very weak.

Further reading: NHS, Diabetes UK, WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region

options: It makes the fast feel longer and raises the risk of dehydration
It is the only meal with salt
quiz.explain: Skipping suhoor makes tiredness and dehydration more likely.

quiz.q: Why should you limit salty foods at suhoor?
quiz.explain: The article explains that salt makes you thirsty during the fast.

quiz.q: What should a person with diabetes do before fasting?
quiz.explain: People with diabetes should talk to their doctor, who may adjust medicine timing.

articles.title: How to Make a Simple Budget That Actually Works
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
A budget is simply a plan for your money. It tells you where your money goes each month, so you can stop wondering why it is gone before the month ends.

You do not need special software or a degree in finance. A notebook, a phone note or a simple spreadsheet is enough.

## Step 1: Know what comes in

Write down all the money you receive in a normal month. This is your income. Include your salary after tax, and any regular extra money, such as a part-time job or family support. If your income changes every month, use a careful, lower number.

## Step 2: Track what goes out

For one month, write down everything you spend, even small things like coffee or a taxi. Then put each item into a group:

- Needs: rent, food, electricity, water, transport, phone, school fees.
- Wants: eating out, new clothes you do not need, games, streaming services.
- Saving and giving: money you put aside, and charity (for example, zakat or sadaqah).

Many people are surprised by how much the small daily costs add up.

## Step 3: Make your plan

Now decide in advance how much goes to each group. One popular starting guide is the "50/30/20" idea: about 50% of income for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for saving. This is only a guide. If your rent is high, your numbers will be different, and that is fine.

A few useful rules:

1. Pay yourself first. Move your saving amount on the day you get paid, before you spend.
2. Give every riyal, dirham, dollar or rupee a job. Income minus planned spending and saving should equal zero.
3. Keep a small "miscellaneous" line for surprises, like a gift or a broken phone screen.

## Step 4: Check and adjust

A budget is not a punishment. At the end of each month, compare your plan with what really happened. If you spent too much on wants, choose one small change, such as cooking at home two more nights a week. Change the plan when your life changes, for example a new job, marriage or a new baby.

Tip: some people use the "envelope" method. They put cash for each group in a separate envelope. When the envelope is empty, spending in that group stops. Phone banking apps often have a similar feature called "pots" or "spaces".

## Key points

- A budget is a plan that shows where your money goes.
- Track your spending for one month before you make the plan.
- Split spending into needs, wants, and saving and giving.
- Save first, on payday, not with what is left over.
- Review your budget every month and adjust it.

Further reading: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), UK MoneyHelper, US Federal Trade Commission (FTC)

options: Track your spending for one month
quiz.explain: The article says to track everything you spend for one month first.

quiz.q: In the 50/30/20 guide, what is the 20% for?
quiz.explain: About 20% of income goes to saving in this guide.

quiz.q: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
options: Move your saving on payday, before spending
quiz.explain: You save first, not with what is left over.

articles.title: Building an Emergency Fund, One Small Step at a Time
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Life brings surprises: a car repair, a doctor's bill or losing a job. An emergency fund is money you keep aside only for these moments, so a bad day does not turn into debt.

Without one, people often borrow from friends, use a credit card or take an expensive loan. With one, you can pay the bill and move on calmly.

## How much do you need?

Many money experts suggest a long-term goal of about three to six months of essential living costs. Essential costs are the things you must pay: rent, food, utilities, transport and basic bills. If your job is less stable, or you are the only earner in your family, you may want more.

That number can feel huge. Do not worry. The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) says the right amount depends on your situation, and that starting small is what matters. A first goal could be enough to cover one surprise bill, such as a car repair. Then build towards one month of costs, and keep going.

## How to build it

1. Choose a target. Write down your monthly essential costs and multiply by three. That is your big goal.
2. Set a small first step, for example a fixed amount every week or every payday.
3. Make it automatic. Ask your bank to move money to a separate account on payday, so you do not have to remember.
4. Add "extra" money. When you receive a bonus, a gift or a tax refund, put part of it in the fund.
5. Cut one small cost, such as a subscription you rarely use, and send that money to the fund instead.

## Where to keep it

The money must be safe and easy to reach quickly, but not so easy that you spend it by accident. A separate savings account at a regulated bank is common. Many readers prefer to avoid interest (riba) for religious reasons. Islamic banks offer savings and current accounts based on Sharia principles, for example accounts where any return comes from shared profit rather than interest. Ask your bank which options it has. Do not keep your emergency fund in risky things like shares or crypto coins, because their value can fall just when you need the money.

## What counts as an emergency?

Ask yourself three questions: Is it unexpected? Is it necessary? Is it urgent? A broken fridge or a sudden medical cost is an emergency. A sale on a new phone is not. If you use the fund, start refilling it as soon as you can.

## Key points

- An emergency fund protects you from debt when surprises happen.
- A common long-term goal is three to six months of essential costs.
- Start small and make saving automatic.
- Keep the money safe and easy to reach, in a separate account.
- Islamic, interest-free savings accounts are available for those who want them.

Further reading: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), UK MoneyHelper, FINRA Investor Education Foundation

quiz.q: What is a common long-term goal for an emergency fund?
options: Three to six months of essential costs
quiz.explain: The article gives three to six months of essential costs as a common goal.

quiz.q: Where should you NOT keep your emergency fund?
options: In a separate bank savings account
In risky shares or crypto coins
quiz.explain: Their value can fall just when you need the money.

quiz.q: Which of these is a real emergency?
options: A sale on a new phone
quiz.explain: It is unexpected, necessary and urgent.

articles.title: Inflation Explained With Everyday Examples
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Have you noticed that the same basket of food costs more than it did a few years ago? That is inflation. Understanding it helps you plan your spending, saving and salary talks.

## What is inflation?

Inflation is the general rise in prices over time. When prices rise, each riyal, pound or dollar buys a little less. Economists call this a fall in "purchasing power", which means how much your money can buy.

Example: if a loaf of bread costs 2.00 this year and 2.10 next year, its price rose by 5%. If most prices rise like this, the inflation rate is about 5%.

## How is it measured?

Government statistics offices track the prices of a "basket" of common things people buy: food, rent, fuel, clothes, transport and more. They compare the cost of this basket over time. The result is often called the Consumer Price Index (CPI). The yearly change in the CPI is the inflation rate you hear about in the news.

Your own inflation can be different. If you drive a lot and fuel prices jump, you feel inflation more than someone who walks to work.

## Why do prices rise?

There are two main causes:

- Demand-pull: people and businesses want to buy more than the economy can produce, so sellers raise prices.
- Cost-push: it becomes more expensive to make or move goods, for example when oil prices rise, so businesses pass the cost on.

Expectations matter too. If everyone expects prices to rise, workers ask for higher pay and shops raise prices early.

Many central banks aim to keep inflation low and steady, often around 2% a year, though some countries set higher targets. A little inflation is considered normal. Very high inflation is harmful, and falling prices for a long time (deflation) can also hurt the economy.

## What inflation means for you

- Cash under the mattress loses value. 1,000 kept at home for five years with 5% yearly inflation will buy roughly what about 780 buys today.
- A pay rise smaller than inflation is really a pay cut in buying power.
- Long-term savings should be planned with inflation in mind.

Simple ways to cope:

1. Review your budget when prices rise, and compare shops.
2. Buy store brands and seasonal food, which are often cheaper.
3. Avoid buying on panic; prices do not always keep rising for the same item.
4. When you discuss pay, know the current inflation rate in your country.

## Key points

- Inflation is the general rise in prices over time.
- It is often measured with a Consumer Price Index (CPI), based on a basket of goods.
- Main causes are high demand and higher costs.
- Many central banks aim for low, steady inflation, often about 2%.
- Inflation slowly reduces the value of cash kept idle.

Further reading: International Monetary Fund (IMF), Bank of England, US Bureau of Labor Statistics

articles.title: How Compound Growth Works, and Halal Ways to Use It
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Compound growth is one of the most powerful ideas in money. It explains why starting to save early, even with small amounts, can make a big difference later.

## The basic idea

Compound growth means you earn growth not only on your original money, but also on the growth you already earned. It is like a snowball rolling downhill: it picks up more snow, so it grows faster and faster.

Example: you put aside 1,000 and it grows by 6% a year.

- After year 1: 1,000 + 60 = 1,060.
- After year 2: 1,060 + 6% = about 1,124. The growth was 64, not 60, because last year's growth also grew.
- After 12 years: about 2,000. The money has roughly doubled.

## The rule of 72

A quick way to estimate doubling time is the "rule of 72". Divide 72 by the yearly growth rate. At 6%, 72 / 6 = 12 years. At 8%, it takes about 9 years. It is only an estimate, but it is useful.

## Time is the secret

Compound growth works best over long periods. Someone who saves a small amount every month from age 25 often ends up with more than someone who saves twice as much from age 40, because the early money has more years to grow.

It works against you too. Debt that charges interest on interest can grow quickly, which is why credit card debt is so dangerous.

## Halal alternatives to interest

Many Muslims avoid interest (riba), because Islam forbids it. Traditional compound interest from a bank deposit is therefore not acceptable to them. But growth itself is not forbidden. Islamic finance aims for returns that come from sharing real business profit and risk, or from trade and real assets. Common examples:

- Mudarabah: you provide money, a bank or business manages it, and profits are shared at an agreed ratio. Losses of money fall on the investor.
- Musharakah: a partnership where partners share profit and loss.
- Sukuk: often called "Islamic bonds", they give a share in a real asset or project and its income.
- Sharia-screened funds that invest in companies whose main business is permitted.

When returns from these are reinvested, they can also compound over time. Returns are not guaranteed, and the value can go down. Always check that a product is approved by a recognised Sharia board and that the provider is regulated. Ask a qualified adviser before investing, and never put in money you cannot afford to lose.

## Key points

- Compound growth means earning growth on earlier growth.
- The rule of 72 estimates how many years money takes to double.
- Starting early matters more than starting big.
- Interest-based debt compounds against you.
- Halal options like mudarabah, musharakah and sukuk can grow through shared profit, but carry risk.

Further reading: US SEC Investor.gov, Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB), Britannica

quiz.explain: 72 divided by 6 equals 12.

options: The money has more years to grow
Banks give bonuses to young savers
quiz.explain: Early money has more time to grow on its growth.

options: From profits shared at an agreed ratio
quiz.explain: Profits are shared at an agreed ratio, not paid as interest.

articles.title: How to Spot Online Scams and Phishing Messages
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Online scams cost people around the world huge amounts of money every year. Scammers are good at sounding real, but most scams follow the same few tricks. Learn them and you can protect yourself and your family.

## What is phishing?

Phishing (said like "fishing") is when criminals send fake emails, text messages, social media messages or phone calls to trick you into giving personal information. They want things like your bank card number, passwords, ID number or one-time codes. They often pretend to be a bank, a delivery company, a government office or even a family member.

## Common warning signs

- Urgency or fear: "Your account will be closed today!" or "You will be fined unless you pay now."
- A prize or gift you did not enter for: "You won a new phone, just pay the delivery fee."
- A request for a code: real banks never ask you to tell them the one-time password (OTP) they send you.
- Strange links or sender addresses: a name that is almost right, such as "paypa1" or extra words in a web address.
- Unusual payment requests: gift cards, crypto coins or money transfers to a personal account.
- Spelling mistakes and an odd greeting like "Dear customer".

Popular scams to know:

1. Fake delivery messages asking you to pay a small fee to release a parcel.
2. "Hi Mum, I lost my phone" messages from a new number, asking for urgent money.
3. Fake job offers that ask you to pay for training or a visa.
4. Investment scams promising big, "guaranteed" returns, often in crypto.
5. Fake shopping websites with prices that are much too good to be true.

## What to do

- Stop and think. Scammers want you to act fast. Take your time.
- Do not click links in unexpected messages. Open your bank's app, or type the official website address yourself.
- Check by calling a number you already know, such as the one on the back of your bank card, not the number in the message.
- For a family member asking for money, call them on their old number or ask a question only they would know.
- Never share passwords or one-time codes with anyone.

## If you were tricked

Act quickly. Call your bank straight away to block cards or payments. Change your passwords. Report the scam to your bank and to your country's official cybercrime or consumer-protection authority. Feeling embarrassed is normal, but scammers trick smart people every day. Reporting helps protect others.

## Key points

- Phishing uses fake messages to steal personal information or money.
- Urgency, prizes and requests for codes are big warning signs.
- Never share one-time codes or passwords.
- Check by contacting the organisation through a number or app you already trust.
- If you are tricked, call your bank and report it immediately.

Further reading: US Federal Trade Commission (FTC), UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), Europol

Contact the organisation using a number or app you already trust

Pressure to act or pay right now
A receipt for something you bought
quiz.explain: Scammers use urgency and fear to rush you.

articles.title: Strong Passwords and Two-Factor Authentication Made Easy
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Your passwords protect your email, bank, photos and messages. If a criminal gets one, they can lock you out, steal money or pretend to be you. A few simple habits make you much safer.

## What makes a password strong?

Length matters more than complex symbols. A long password is much harder for computers to guess. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) recommends joining three random words, for example "applenemobiro" (apple + nemo + biro, its own example; do not use it). You can add numbers or symbols if a website asks for them.

Avoid:

- Personal details: names, birthdays, phone numbers, your football team.
- Common passwords like "123456", "password" or "qwerty".
- Simple patterns, such as changing "Riyadh1" to "Riyadh2".

## One account, one password

The biggest danger is using the same password everywhere. Websites sometimes get hacked and passwords leak. Criminals then try that same email and password on many other sites. If you reuse passwords, one leak can open all your accounts.

Your email password is the most important. If someone controls your email, they can reset the passwords for your other accounts. Give it a strong, unique password.

## Let a password manager help

Nobody can remember dozens of long passwords. A password manager is an app that creates and stores strong passwords for you, locked behind one main password. Many phones and web browsers have one built in. Security agencies such as the NCSC recommend them.

## Turn on two-factor authentication

Two-factor authentication (2FA), also called two-step verification, adds a second check after your password. It can be:

1. A code sent by text message.
2. A code from an authenticator app on your phone.
3. A tap on a prompt in a trusted app, or a fingerprint or face check.
4. A small physical security key.

Even if a criminal steals your password, they usually cannot get in without the second step. Turn on 2FA first for email, banking and social media. Look in the account's "Security" or "Login" settings. An app or security key is generally safer than a text message, but any 2FA is far better than none.

Good daily habits:

- Never tell anyone a password or a 2FA code, even someone claiming to be from the company.
- Lock your phone with a PIN, fingerprint or face check.
- Install updates for your phone and apps; they often fix security holes.
- If a site tells you about a data leak, change that password at once.

## Key points

- Long passwords are stronger; three random words is an easy method.
- Use a different password for every important account, especially email.
- A password manager can create and remember passwords for you.
- Turn on two-factor authentication for email, banking and social media.
- Never share passwords or codes with anyone.

Further reading: UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

quiz.explain: The NCSC suggests joining three random words.

quiz.explain: Criminals try leaked passwords on many other sites.

options: A second check after your password
quiz.explain: 2FA adds a second step, like a code or fingerprint.

articles.title: Study Techniques That Really Work: Active Recall and Spacing
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Many students spend hours rereading notes and highlighting, then forget most of it in the exam. Research shows that a few simple changes can help you remember much more in the same time.

In 2013, a group of psychologists led by John Dunlosky reviewed hundreds of studies on ten popular study methods. Two methods came out on top: practice testing and spacing out your study. Rereading and highlighting were rated low.

## 1. Active recall (practice testing)

Active recall means pulling information out of your memory, instead of just looking at it again. Each time you remember something, the memory becomes stronger.

How to do it:

- Close the book and write down everything you remember about the topic. Then check what you missed.
- Make flashcards: a question on one side, the answer on the other.
- Answer past exam papers or the questions at the end of a chapter.
- Explain the topic out loud, as if teaching a friend.

It feels harder than rereading. That effort is a good sign: it means your brain is working.

## 2. Spaced repetition (distributed practice)

Spaced repetition means studying the same material several times, with gaps in between, rather than cramming it all into one long night. Forgetting a little between sessions and then remembering again makes the memory last longer.

A simple plan: review new material one day later, then a few days later, then a week later, then a few weeks later. Flashcard apps can schedule this for you automatically. Even without an app, you can use a box with sections: cards you get right move to a section you review less often.

## 3. Helpful extras

- Mix topics (interleaving). Instead of 30 maths problems of one type, mix different types. This helps you learn to choose the right method.
- Ask "why?" and "how?" while you read, and connect new ideas to what you know.
- Sleep well. Sleep helps the brain store what you learned during the day.
- Remove distractions. Put your phone in another room during study blocks.

## A sample study session

1. 5 minutes: look over the topic headings.
2. 20 minutes: study one section.
3. 10 minutes: close notes, write or say what you remember, then check.
4. Short break, then repeat with a new section.
5. Next day: quiz yourself on yesterday's material before starting anything new.

## Key points

- Testing yourself (active recall) is one of the best ways to learn.
- Spread study over several days instead of cramming.
- Rereading and highlighting alone are weak methods.
- Mixing topics, asking "why", and good sleep all help.
- Effortful study feels harder but works better.

Further reading: Association for Psychological Science (Dunlosky et al., 2013), Kent State University, Learning Scientists

quiz.explain: Practice testing and distributed practice were rated high utility.

options: Pulling information out of your memory
quiz.explain: Active recall means remembering without looking.

quiz.q: What does spaced repetition mean?
options: Taking long breaks with no study
Reviewing material several times with gaps between
quiz.explain: You review the same material again after gaps of time.

articles.title: Writing a Good CV and Getting Ready for a Job Interview
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Your CV (curriculum vitae, also called a resume) is often an employer's first look at you. A clear CV gets you to the interview, and good preparation helps you do well once you are there.

## What to put in your CV

A typical CV has these parts:

1. Contact details: full name, phone number, a professional email address and your city. A photo, age or marital status is common in some countries but not expected in others, so follow local custom.
2. Personal profile: 2 to 4 sentences about who you are, your main skills and the kind of job you want.
3. Work experience: newest job first. For each one, give the job title, employer, dates and 2 to 4 points on what you did.
4. Education and training: degrees, diplomas, courses and certificates.
5. Skills: languages, computer programs and other useful abilities.

## Tips for a strong CV

- Keep it short. One or two pages is usual for most jobs.
- Show results, not only duties. "Served customers" is weak. "Handled about 50 customer requests a day with high satisfaction scores" is stronger.
- Start points with action words like "organised", "built", "trained" or "improved".
- Change your CV for each job. Read the job advert and use its key words where they are true for you. Many companies use software that scans CVs for these words.
- Check spelling and grammar carefully, and ask a friend to read it.
- Be honest. Never invent degrees or jobs; employers check.

## Preparing for the interview

Research the company: what it does, its products and its recent news. Read the job advert again and think about how your experience matches each point.

Prepare answers to common questions:

- "Tell me about yourself." Give a short summary of your background, skills and why you want this job.
- "What are your strengths and weaknesses?" For a weakness, choose a real one and explain how you are improving it.
- "Why do you want to work here?"

For questions like "Tell me about a time you solved a problem", use the STAR method:

- Situation: what was happening?
- Task: what did you need to do?
- Action: what did you do?
- Result: what happened, and what did you learn?

## On the day

Arrive 10 to 15 minutes early, or test your camera and internet before an online interview. Dress neatly. Listen carefully, and ask for a question to be repeated if needed. At the end, ask one or two questions of your own, such as "What does success look like in this role?" Afterwards, a short thank-you email is a polite touch.

## Key points

- A CV should be clear, honest and usually one or two pages.
- Show results and use action words.
- Adjust your CV for each job advert.
- Research the company and practise common questions.
- Use the STAR method to answer questions about past experiences.

Further reading: UK National Careers Service, Harvard University Career Services, US Department of Labor (CareerOneStop)

quiz.explain: STAR is Situation, Task, Action, Result.

quiz.explain: The article says one or two pages is usual.

options: To match the job advert's key words where true
To add jobs you never had
Because employers want a new photo
quiz.explain: Using the advert's key words honestly helps your CV match the job.

articles.title: How Desalination Turns Seawater Into Drinking Water
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
In much of the Gulf, the water from your tap started its life in the sea. Desalination makes this possible, and knowing how it works helps you see why saving water still matters.

## What is desalination?

Desalination means removing salt from water. Seawater has about 35 grams of salt in every litre. That is far too salty to drink or to grow crops. Desalination plants take out almost all of this salt and make fresh water.

Countries with little rain and few rivers depend on it. Saudi Arabia is one of the largest producers of desalinated water in the world, and big cities such as Jeddah and Makkah get most of their water from plants on the coast. Other Gulf states also rely on it heavily.

## Method 1: Boiling (thermal desalination)

The oldest method copies nature. When the sun heats the sea, water rises as vapour (gas) and the salt stays behind. Later the vapour falls as rain, which is fresh.

Thermal plants do the same thing faster:
1. Seawater is heated until it turns into steam.
2. The steam is moved away from the salty water.
3. The steam is cooled, so it turns back into liquid fresh water.

Many older Gulf plants are built next to power stations and use their spare heat. But boiling water needs a lot of energy.

## Method 2: Reverse osmosis

Most new plants use reverse osmosis. A membrane is a very thin sheet with tiny holes. The holes let water molecules pass but block salt.

1. Seawater is first cleaned of sand, mud and living things.
2. Strong pumps push the water against the membrane at high pressure.
3. Fresh water passes through. Salt is left behind.
4. Small amounts of minerals are added back, and the water is disinfected so it is safe and tastes good.

Reverse osmosis usually uses much less energy than boiling, so many countries are switching to it.

## The costs and challenges

Desalination is not free or perfect:
- Energy: plants need a lot of electricity, often from oil or gas. Some new plants use solar power to cut pollution.
- Brine: the leftover water is very salty. If it is poured back into the sea carelessly, it can harm fish and coral.
- Money: desalinated water costs more to make than water from rivers or wells.

This is why saving water at home still matters, even when the tap never runs dry. Fix leaks, take shorter showers, and turn off the tap while brushing your teeth.

## Key points

- Desalination removes salt from seawater to make drinking water.
- Thermal plants boil seawater and collect the steam.
- Reverse osmosis pushes water through a fine membrane that blocks salt.
- It needs a lot of energy and leaves salty brine, so saving water still helps.

Further reading: US Geological Survey (USGS), Britannica, Saudi Water Authority, Arab News

quiz.explain: The membrane's tiny holes let water pass but stop salt.

quiz.explain: The very salty leftover water is called brine.

quiz.explain: Making fresh water from the sea is costly and energy-hungry.

articles.title: How Solar Panels Turn Sunlight Into Electricity
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Solar panels are appearing on rooftops, farms and deserts around the world. Understanding how they work helps you judge whether solar could lower your own electricity bills.

## Sunlight is energy

Sunlight is made of tiny packets of energy called photons. Every second, the Sun sends huge amounts of this energy to Earth. A solar panel catches some of it and turns it into electricity.

## Inside a solar cell

A solar panel is made of many small solar cells. Most cells are made of silicon, the same material found in sand and in computer chips.

Here is what happens, step by step:
1. Sunlight hits the silicon cell.
2. The photons give energy to tiny particles called electrons, knocking them loose.
3. The cell is built in two layers that push the free electrons in one direction.
4. Metal lines on the cell collect the moving electrons. Moving electrons are an electric current.

This is called the photovoltaic effect. "Photo" means light and "voltaic" means electricity.

Most home panels turn roughly one-fifth of the sunlight that hits them into electricity. The rest becomes heat or bounces away.

## From the roof to your home

Solar cells make direct current (DC), where electricity flows one way. Homes use alternating current (AC). So a device called an inverter changes DC into AC.

The electricity can then:
- Power your lights and appliances right away.
- Charge a battery, so you can use it at night.
- Flow into the public grid. In some places the power company pays or credits you for it.

Large solar farms work the same way, just with thousands of panels.

## Strengths and limits

Good points:
- Sunlight is free and never runs out.
- Panels make no smoke or noise while working.
- Panels often last 25 years or more.

Limits:
- No sunlight at night, and less on cloudy days.
- Dust and sand reduce output. In desert countries panels need regular cleaning.
- Very high heat slightly lowers a panel's efficiency.


Tips if you are thinking about solar:
- Check how much sun your roof gets and whether it faces the right way.
- Compare quotes from several trusted installers.
- Ask about local rules, permits and any government support.
- Clean panels gently with water, and never climb on a roof without proper safety gear.

## Key points

- Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity using the photovoltaic effect.
- Light knocks electrons loose in silicon, creating an electric current.
- An inverter changes the panel's DC power into AC for the home.
- Solar works best in sunny places, but dust, night and clouds reduce output.

Further reading: US Department of Energy, NASA, Britannica, International Energy Agency

quiz.q: What is the photovoltaic effect?
options: Light creating electricity in a material
quiz.explain: Photo means light and voltaic means electricity.

quiz.q: What does an inverter do?
options: Changes DC electricity into AC electricity
quiz.explain: Homes use AC, so the inverter converts the panel's DC.

quiz.q: Why do panels in desert countries need regular cleaning?
options: Dust and sand reduce their output
Cleaning makes them cooler at night
quiz.explain: A layer of dust blocks sunlight from the cells.

articles.title: How GPS Knows Exactly Where You Are
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Every time you open a map on your phone or order a taxi, GPS is working for you. It is free, works almost everywhere on Earth, and relies on clever science.

## What is GPS?

GPS stands for Global Positioning System. It was built and is run by the United States. It has three parts:
- Satellites: about 30 working satellites circle the Earth, roughly 20,000 kilometres up. Each one goes around the planet about twice a day.
- Ground stations: these track the satellites and correct their data.
- Receivers: the small chip in your phone, car or watch.

Other countries run similar systems: Europe's Galileo, Russia's GLONASS and China's BeiDou. Most modern phones use several of them together, which makes them more accurate.


Each satellite carries very precise atomic clocks. It sends out a radio signal again and again saying: "I am this satellite, this is where I am, and this is the exact time."

Your phone does not send anything back to the satellites. It only listens.

## Measuring distance with time

Radio signals travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second. Your phone checks how long each signal took to arrive. Time multiplied by speed gives the distance to that satellite.

## Finding your spot

Knowing your distance from one satellite places you somewhere on a giant sphere (ball) around it. Distances from more satellites narrow this down:
1. One satellite: you are somewhere on a large sphere.
2. Two satellites: the spheres cross in a circle.
3. Three satellites: the circle shrinks to a point.
4. A fourth satellite corrects the small error in your phone's cheaper clock.

This method is called trilateration. Because signals travel so fast, a tiny timing error of one millionth of a second would put you about 300 metres off. That is why exact time is so important.

Scientists must even correct the satellite clocks for Einstein's theory of relativity. Without this, positions would drift by kilometres each day.

## Getting the best signal

- GPS works best outdoors with a clear view of the sky.
- Tall buildings, tunnels and thick roofs can block or bounce signals.
- Phones also use Wi-Fi and mobile towers to help, especially indoors.
- Turn location on only for apps that need it, to protect your privacy and battery.

## Key points

- GPS uses about 30 satellites that send exact time signals.
- Your phone only listens; it measures how long signals take to arrive.
- Signals from at least four satellites give your position.
- Precise clocks, even corrected for relativity, make GPS accurate.

Further reading: GPS.gov (US government), NASA, European Space Agency, Britannica

quiz.explain: GPS receivers only listen to satellite signals.

quiz.q: How does your phone work out its distance to a satellite?
options: By measuring how long the signal took to arrive
quiz.explain: Travel time multiplied by the speed of light gives the distance.

quiz.q: Why is a fourth satellite needed?
options: To correct the error in the phone's clock
quiz.explain: The fourth signal fixes the small error in your phone's less precise clock.

articles.title: How Vaccines Train Your Immune System
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Vaccines have helped wipe out smallpox and made many deadly childhood diseases rare. Knowing how they work helps you make calm, informed choices for your family.

## Your body's defence team

Your immune system protects you from germs such as viruses and bacteria. When a new germ enters your body, the immune system learns to fight it. It makes antibodies. These are proteins that stick to the germ and help destroy it.

The problem is time. The first time you meet a germ, your body can take days or weeks to build a strong defence. During that time, you can become very sick.

## A safe practice session

A vaccine gives your immune system a safe practice run. It contains a harmless piece or version of a germ, or instructions for your cells to make one harmless piece of it. This part is called an antigen. It looks like the germ to your immune system but cannot cause the full disease.

Common types of vaccines include:
- Inactivated vaccines, made from germs that have been killed.
- Weakened (live attenuated) vaccines, made from germs too weak to cause serious illness in healthy people.
- Subunit vaccines, which contain just one part of the germ, such as a protein.
- mRNA vaccines, which give your cells short-lived instructions to make one harmless germ protein.


After vaccination, your body makes antibodies and also special memory cells. Memory cells remember the germ for months or years. If the real germ arrives later, they recognise it quickly and your body fights back fast, often before you get sick.

Some vaccines need several doses or later boosters to keep this memory strong.

## Protecting others too

When most people in a community are vaccinated, germs find it hard to spread. This protects people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies or people with certain illnesses. This is called community or herd immunity.

## What to expect

- A sore arm, mild fever or tiredness for a day or two is common. It is a sign the body is learning.
- Serious side effects are rare. Health staff watch for them.
- Keep your family's vaccination record safe and follow your country's official schedule.
- Ask a doctor or nurse if you have questions, are pregnant, or have a weak immune system.

See a doctor quickly if someone has trouble breathing, swelling of the face, or a high fever after a vaccine.

## Key points

- Vaccines show your immune system a harmless version or part of a germ.
- Your body makes antibodies and memory cells against it.
- If the real germ comes later, your body fights it quickly.
- High vaccination rates also protect people who cannot be vaccinated.

Further reading: World Health Organization (WHO), US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), NHS
