options: Cells that remember a germ so the body can react quickly later
quiz.explain: Memory cells recognise the germ fast if it returns.

quiz.q: What is an antigen in a vaccine?
options: A harmless piece or version of a germ that trains the immune system
quiz.explain: The antigen looks like the germ but cannot cause the full disease.

quiz.q: What is community (herd) immunity?
options: When many people are vaccinated, germs spread less and others are protected
quiz.explain: High vaccination rates make it hard for germs to spread.

articles.title: How Antibiotics Work and Why Resistance Is Dangerous
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Antibiotics have saved hundreds of millions of lives. But when they are misused, they stop working. How you use them today affects whether they work for your children tomorrow.

## What antibiotics do

Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from multiplying. Bacteria are tiny living things. Most are harmless, but some cause infections such as strep throat, urinary infections or some kinds of pneumonia.

Antibiotics attack parts that bacteria have but human cells do not. For example, some break down the bacteria's outer wall. Others stop bacteria from making the proteins they need to grow.

Antibiotics do not work against viruses. Colds, flu and most sore throats and coughs are caused by viruses. Taking antibiotics for them will not help you get better faster, and it can cause side effects.

## How resistance happens

Bacteria multiply very fast. Sometimes, by chance, a few bacteria have a change that lets them survive an antibiotic. When the medicine kills the others, these tough survivors are left to multiply. They can spread to other people. Over time, the antibiotic stops working against them.

This is called antibiotic resistance. Bacteria that resist many antibiotics are sometimes called "superbugs".

Resistance grows faster when antibiotics are:
- Taken for viral illnesses like colds.
- Stopped early, or taken without a prescription.
- Shared with others or saved for later.
- Overused in farm animals.

## Why it matters

A large study published in The Lancet estimated that about 1.27 million deaths in 2019 were directly caused by drug-resistant bacterial infections. The World Health Organization calls resistance one of the top global threats to public health.

When antibiotics fail, simple infections become hard to treat. Surgery, cancer treatment and childbirth become riskier, because they depend on antibiotics to prevent infection.

## What you can do

1. Take antibiotics only when a qualified doctor prescribes them.
2. Follow the doctor's instructions exactly, including how long to take them.
3. Never share antibiotics or use leftover pills.
4. Do not pressure your doctor for antibiotics for a cold or flu.
5. Prevent infections: wash your hands with soap, keep food clean and cooked well, and keep vaccines up to date.

See a doctor if a fever lasts more than a few days, if you have trouble breathing, or if an infection gets worse instead of better.

## Key points

- Antibiotics kill bacteria but do not work on viruses like colds and flu.
- Misuse helps resistant bacteria survive and spread.
- Resistance makes common infections and surgery more dangerous.
- Use antibiotics only as prescribed, and help prevent infections.

Further reading: World Health Organization (WHO), US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), The Lancet, NHS

quiz.q: Do antibiotics work against colds and flu?
options: No, because colds and flu are caused by viruses
quiz.explain: Antibiotics only work against bacteria, not viruses.

quiz.q: How does antibiotic resistance develop?
options: Bacteria that survive the medicine multiply and spread
The medicine gets old in the box
quiz.explain: Tough survivors multiply when the others are killed.

quiz.q: Which habit helps slow resistance?
options: Taking antibiotics only as a doctor prescribes
Stopping as soon as you feel better without asking
quiz.explain: Using antibiotics exactly as prescribed reduces misuse.

articles.title: How Earthquakes Happen and How to Stay Safe
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Earthquakes strike without warning and can be deadly. Knowing why they happen, and what to do in the first seconds, can protect you and your family.

## The Earth's moving puzzle

The outer shell of the Earth is broken into giant pieces called tectonic plates. They fit together like a cracked eggshell. The plates float on hotter, softer rock below and move very slowly, a few centimetres a year. That is about as fast as your fingernails grow.

Places where plates meet are called plate boundaries. Plates can:
- Push into each other, building mountains.
- Pull apart, letting new rock rise up.
- Slide past each other sideways.

## Why the ground shakes

Plates do not slide smoothly. Their edges are rough and get stuck. A crack in the rock where movement happens is called a fault.

1. The plates keep moving, but the stuck edges cannot.
2. Stress builds up in the rocks for years or even centuries, like a bending stick.
3. Suddenly the rock breaks or slips.
4. The stored energy rushes out as waves, called seismic waves.

These waves travel through the ground and make it shake. The point underground where the slip starts is the focus. The spot on the surface directly above it is the epicentre.

## Measuring earthquakes

Scientists measure size with the magnitude scale. Each step up means much more energy. A magnitude 7 earthquake releases about 32 times more energy than a magnitude 6. Small quakes happen every day and most are never felt.

Large earthquakes under the sea can push up water and cause tsunamis. These are giant, fast waves that can flood coasts.

The Arabian Plate, for example, is slowly moving away from Africa, which is opening the Red Sea and pushing against Iran, where earthquakes are common.

## What to do in an earthquake

Indoors, follow "Drop, Cover and Hold On":
1. Drop to your hands and knees.
2. Cover your head and neck, ideally under a strong table.
3. Hold on until the shaking stops.

Also:
- Stay away from windows and heavy objects that can fall.
- Do not run outside during shaking.
- If outdoors, move away from buildings, wires and trees.
- Near the coast, if shaking is strong or long, move to high ground quickly in case of a tsunami.


Prepare before it happens:
- Fix heavy furniture and shelves to walls.
- Keep water, a torch, a first-aid kit and medicines ready.
- Agree on a family meeting place.

## Key points

- Earthquakes happen when stuck tectonic plates suddenly slip along a fault.
- The released energy travels as seismic waves that shake the ground.
- Each step on the magnitude scale means about 32 times more energy.
- In a quake, Drop, Cover and Hold On, and stay away from windows.

Further reading: US Geological Survey (USGS), Britannica, Ready.gov, Red Cross

quiz.q: What causes most earthquakes?
quiz.explain: Stress builds at stuck plate edges and is released suddenly.

quiz.q: How much more energy does a magnitude 7 quake release than a magnitude 6?
quiz.explain: Each step on the scale means about 32 times more energy.

quiz.q: What should you do indoors during an earthquake?
quiz.explain: Drop, Cover and Hold On protects you from falling objects.

articles.title: How Undersea Cables Carry Your Messages Around the World
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
When you send a message to a friend in another continent, it probably does not go through space. It most likely travels along the bottom of the ocean. Knowing this helps you understand why internet outages sometimes hit whole regions.

## The hidden internet

Many people think the internet travels mainly by satellite. In fact, most data between continents moves through submarine (undersea) cables. Experts estimate these cables carry the large majority of international internet traffic, often said to be about 95 to 99 percent.

There are more than 500 of these cables around the world. Some are short, linking nearby countries. Others stretch across whole oceans.

## What is inside a cable?

In deep water, a cable is about as thick as a garden hose. Inside are:
- Optical fibres: hair-thin strands of very pure glass that carry data as light.
- Layers of plastic, steel and copper that protect the fibres and carry power.

Near the shore, where ships and fishing nets are a danger, cables have extra armour and are often buried under the seabed.

## How light carries your message

1. Your phone turns your message into digital data: a long list of 1s and 0s.
2. The data reaches a coastal building called a landing station.
3. Lasers turn the 1s and 0s into very fast flashes of light.
4. The light travels along the glass fibres, bouncing inside them.
5. Every so often, devices called repeaters boost the light so it stays strong.
6. On the other side, the light is turned back into data and sent on to your friend.

All of this takes only a fraction of a second.


Cables beat satellites in three ways:
- They carry far more data.
- They are faster, because the signal does not travel to space and back.
- They are cheaper per amount of data sent.

Satellites are still very useful for ships, planes and remote areas without cables.

## When cables break

Cables are sometimes damaged, mostly by ship anchors and fishing gear, and sometimes by earthquakes. Special repair ships find the broken part, lift it up and join it again. This can take days or weeks.

The Red Sea and the Gulf are important routes for cables between Europe, Asia and Africa. Damage there can slow the internet in many countries at once. Networks usually have several routes, so traffic can be sent another way.

## Key points

- Most data between continents travels through undersea cables, not satellites.
- Cables use glass optical fibres that carry data as flashes of light.
- Repeaters boost the signal along the way.
- Damage from anchors or earthquakes can slow the internet across whole regions.

Further reading: Smithsonian Magazine, TeleGeography, Britannica, International Telecommunication Union (ITU)

quiz.q: How does most data travel between continents?
quiz.explain: Undersea cables carry the large majority of international traffic.

quiz.q: What carries the data inside the cable?
quiz.explain: Optical fibres carry data as flashes of light.

quiz.q: What most often damages undersea cables?
quiz.explain: Most damage comes from anchors and fishing gear.

articles.title: Black Holes Explained Simply
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Black holes sound like science fiction, but they are real and there is one at the centre of our own galaxy. Learning about them is a great way to understand gravity, the force that shapes the whole universe.

## What is a black hole?

A black hole is a place in space where gravity is so strong that nothing can escape, not even light. Because no light comes out, we cannot see a black hole directly. That is why it is called "black".

The reason is that a huge amount of matter (stuff) is squeezed into a very small space. The more tightly matter is packed, the stronger its pull nearby.

## How black holes form

Many black holes are born when a very large star dies:
1. A big star burns its fuel for millions of years.
2. When the fuel runs out, the star can no longer hold itself up.
3. Its centre collapses under its own weight.
4. The outer layers can blast away in a huge explosion called a supernova.
5. If the collapsed centre is heavy enough, it becomes a black hole.

Our Sun is far too small to ever become a black hole.


- Stellar black holes are made from dead stars. They may weigh several to dozens of times as much as the Sun.
- Supermassive black holes sit at the centres of most large galaxies. They weigh millions or even billions of Suns.

Our galaxy, the Milky Way, has a supermassive black hole at its centre called Sagittarius A*. It weighs about 4 million Suns and is about 26,000 light-years away, so it is no danger to Earth.

## The edge of no return

Around every black hole is a boundary called the event horizon. Outside it, things can still escape if they move fast enough. Once anything crosses it, there is no way back.

Gas swirling around a black hole gets extremely hot and glows brightly before falling in. This glow is how scientists find many black holes.

## How do we know they exist?

- Scientists watch stars orbiting very fast around something invisible and heavy.
- In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope, a team linking radio telescopes around the world, shared the first image of a black hole's shadow, in the galaxy M87. In 2022 it shared an image of Sagittarius A*.
- Detectors on Earth have measured gravitational waves, tiny ripples in space made when black holes crash together.

## Key points

- A black hole's gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.
- Many form when a very large star collapses at the end of its life.
- The event horizon is the boundary of no return.
- Our galaxy has a supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, far from Earth.

Further reading: NASA, European Space Agency, Event Horizon Telescope, Britannica

quiz.q: Why can't we see a black hole directly?
options: It is too far to ever study
Not even light can escape it
It is always behind the Sun
quiz.explain: Its gravity traps light, so it looks black.

quiz.q: What is the event horizon?
options: The boundary beyond which nothing can escape
The place where stars are born
quiz.explain: Once something crosses the event horizon, there is no way back.

quiz.q: What is Sagittarius A*?
options: The supermassive black hole at the centre of our galaxy
quiz.explain: It weighs about 4 million Suns and sits at the Milky Way's centre.

articles.title: The House of Wisdom and the Islamic Golden Age of Science
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Many words you use every day, like "algebra" and "algorithm", come from Arabic scholars who worked more than 1,000 years ago. Knowing this story helps you see how knowledge moves between cultures, and how much modern science owes to many peoples.

## What was the House of Wisdom?

The House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikmah in Arabic) was a library and centre of learning in Baghdad, the capital of the Abbasid caliphate. A caliphate is a state led by a caliph, a Muslim ruler. It began as a royal library, probably under Caliph Harun al-Rashid (ruled 786 to 809). It grew much bigger under his son al-Ma'mun (ruled 813 to 833).

Scholars of many backgrounds worked there: Muslims, Christians, Jews and others. They spoke Arabic, Persian, Greek and Syriac.

## The great translation movement

A key job was translation. Scholars translated books on medicine, mathematics, astronomy and philosophy from Greek, Persian and Indian sources into Arabic. One famous translator was Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a Christian doctor who translated many Greek medical works.

This work saved many old books that might otherwise have been lost. Paper also helped. Paper-making had come from China, and Baghdad had paper mills by the late 700s, so books became cheaper to copy.

## Famous scholars and ideas

The Golden Age spread far beyond one building, to cities such as Cairo, Damascus, Córdoba and Bukhara. Some names to know:

- Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book whose title gave us the word "algebra". His name, in Latin form, gave us "algorithm". He also helped spread the Hindu-Arabic numbers we use today.
- Ibn al-Haytham, working in Cairo, studied light and vision. He stressed testing ideas with careful experiments.
- Ibn Sina (Avicenna) wrote "The Canon of Medicine", which was used in European universities for centuries.

## How did it end?

In 1258, Mongol armies captured Baghdad. Many people were killed, and libraries, including the House of Wisdom, were destroyed. Historians say many books were thrown into the Tigris River. But the ideas survived. Many Arabic books were later translated into Latin in Spain and Sicily, and they helped Europe's later scientific growth.

## Key points

- The House of Wisdom was a centre of learning in Abbasid Baghdad, expanded under al-Ma'mun.
- Scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and added new discoveries.
- Words like "algebra" and "algorithm" come from this period.
- Baghdad was destroyed by the Mongols in 1258, but the knowledge passed on to other lands.

A simple tip: next time you use a calculator or a computer, remember that its basic ideas have roots in many cultures, including this one.

Further reading: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Library of Congress, Science Museum Group

quiz.q: In which city was the House of Wisdom?
quiz.explain: The House of Wisdom was in Baghdad, the Abbasid capital.

quiz.q: Which English word comes from al-Khwarizmi's name?
quiz.explain: His name in Latin form gave us the word algorithm.

quiz.q: What happened in Baghdad in 1258?
options: The House of Wisdom was founded
quiz.explain: In 1258 Mongol armies captured Baghdad and destroyed its libraries.

articles.title: How Saudi Arabia Was Unified, 1902 to 1932
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Every year on 23 September, Saudi Arabia celebrates its National Day. This guide explains, in simple terms, the 30 years of events behind that date and how a divided region became one country.

## Before 1902

At the start of the 1900s, the Arabian Peninsula was split between many rulers. The Al Rashid family controlled much of central and northern Arabia from Ha'il. The Hejaz, the western region with Mecca and Medina, was ruled by the Hashemite Sharif of Mecca under Ottoman rule. The Ottoman Empire also held parts of the east. The Al Saud family had ruled earlier Saudi states, but in the 1890s it lost Riyadh and lived in exile in Kuwait.

Saudi Arabia also marks Founding Day on 22 February. It remembers the first Saudi state, started in 1727 by Imam Muhammad bin Saud.

## The return to Riyadh (1902)

In January 1902, the young Abdulaziz bin Abdulrahman Al Saud, often called Ibn Saud, led a small group of men from Kuwait and took back Riyadh. This is seen as the start of the modern Saudi state.

## Step by step

Over the next three decades, the territory grew through military campaigns, local alliances and agreements with tribes:

1. 1913: the eastern region of al-Ahsa was taken from Ottoman control.
2. 1921: Ha'il was taken, ending the Al Rashid state.
3. 1924 to 1925: the Hejaz, including Mecca, Medina and Jeddah, came under Abdulaziz's rule after war with the Hashemites.
4. 1926: Abdulaziz was declared King of the Hejaz. In 1927 he also became King of Najd.
5. 1927: in the Treaty of Jeddah, Britain recognised his rule as independent.
6. 23 September 1932: the lands were joined under one name, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

## Different views and what came next

Saudi histories describe this period as a time of unification that brought security and an end to raids between tribes. Other groups saw it differently. The Hashemites lost the Hejaz, and some tribes and rival families lost power. Even some of Abdulaziz's own former allies, the Ikhwan fighters, rebelled in the late 1920s and were defeated in 1929. Like most state-building, it involved both agreement and conflict.

Oil was found in commercial amounts at Dammam in 1938. This changed the country's economy in the following decades. King Abdulaziz ruled until his death in 1953, and his sons have ruled since.

## Key points

- The modern Saudi story starts with the return to Riyadh in January 1902.
- The Hejaz came under Saudi rule in 1924 to 1925.
- The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was named on 23 September 1932, now National Day.
- Founding Day (22 February) remembers the first Saudi state in 1727.

Further reading: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Saudipedia, Library of Congress Country Studies

quiz.q: What date is Saudi National Day?
quiz.explain: The kingdom was named on 23 September 1932, now National Day.

quiz.q: When did Abdulaziz take back Riyadh?
quiz.explain: He retook Riyadh in January 1902.

quiz.q: What does Founding Day remember?
quiz.explain: Founding Day marks the first Saudi state, started in 1727.

articles.title: The Silk Road: How Trade Linked East and West
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Today, goods move around the world by ship and plane. Long before that, a network of land and sea routes called the Silk Road joined China, Central Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Europe. Its story shows how trade spreads not only goods, but also ideas, foods and even diseases.

## What was the Silk Road?

The Silk Road was not one road. It was a web of many routes, thousands of kilometres long, used for about 1,500 years. Very few traders travelled the whole way. Instead, goods passed from merchant to merchant, city to city, like a relay race.

The name is quite new. A German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, made it popular in 1877. Historians often date the start of regular trade to the Han dynasty of China, around the 2nd century BCE, when the envoy Zhang Qian travelled west.

## What moved along it?

- Goods: silk, tea and porcelain from China; spices from India and Southeast Asia; horses, glass, wool, gold and silver from the west.
- Technologies: paper-making and, later, gunpowder spread west from China.
- Religions and ideas: Buddhism spread into China. Islam, Christianity and other faiths spread along the routes too.
- Diseases: in the 1300s, the plague known as the Black Death is thought to have travelled along these trade networks.

## Famous cities and travellers

Cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara (in today's Uzbekistan), Merv, Baghdad and Kashgar grew rich as trading stops. Caravanserais, roadside inns for camel caravans, gave travellers a safe place to rest.

Two famous travellers wrote about these lands. Marco Polo, from Venice, described his travels to China in the late 1200s. Ibn Battuta, from Morocco, travelled across the Muslim world, India and China in the 1300s.

## Why did it decline?

From the late 1400s, European sailors found sea routes around Africa to Asia. Ships could carry more goods at lower cost, so long land routes became less important. Wars and the breakup of large empires also made travel harder.

## Key points

- The Silk Road was a network of land and sea routes, not a single road.
- It carried goods, technologies, religions and diseases.
- The name "Silk Road" was made popular in 1877.
- Sea trade from the late 1400s reduced its importance.

A practical thought: many things on your table today, from rice to spices, have travelled along routes like these. Trade has always connected people.

Further reading: UNESCO, Encyclopaedia Britannica, National Geographic

quiz.q: What was the Silk Road?
options: A network of land and sea routes
quiz.explain: It was a web of many routes, not one road.

quiz.q: Which technology spread west from China along the routes?
quiz.explain: Paper-making spread west from China.

quiz.q: Why did the Silk Road become less important?
quiz.explain: From the late 1400s, ships carried goods more cheaply.

articles.title: Al-Andalus: Nearly 800 Years of Muslim Spain
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
The beautiful Alhambra palace in Granada and the Great Mosque of Córdoba still attract millions of visitors. They are reminders of al-Andalus, the name for the parts of Spain and Portugal under Muslim rule from 711 to 1492. Its story is one of science, art and shared cultures, but also of war.

## How it began

In 711, an army led by Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from North Africa into Spain. The rock of Gibraltar takes its name from him: "Jabal Tariq", the mountain of Tariq. Within a few years, most of the Iberian Peninsula (today's Spain and Portugal) was under Muslim rule.

In 756, Abd al-Rahman I, a member of the Umayyad family who had escaped from the Middle East, set up an independent state with its capital in Córdoba. In 929, Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph.

## A centre of learning

At its height, Córdoba was one of the largest and most advanced cities in Europe. It had libraries, paved streets and public baths. Famous thinkers included:

- Ibn Rushd (Averroes), a philosopher whose writings on Aristotle shaped European thought.
- Al-Zahrawi, a surgeon whose medical book described many surgical tools.
- Maimonides, a Jewish philosopher and doctor born in Córdoba.

Many Arabic books were translated into Latin in cities such as Toledo, which helped carry knowledge into the rest of Europe.

## Living together?

Muslims, Christians and Jews lived side by side in al-Andalus. Some historians use the Spanish word "convivencia" (living together) for this. Others say the picture was more mixed. Non-Muslims had protected status but paid a special tax and faced limits. There were periods of tolerance and periods of tension and violence. Both views have evidence.

## The long end

After 1031 the caliphate broke into small kingdoms called taifas. Christian kingdoms in the north slowly took land in a long process later called the Reconquista. Granada, ruled by the Nasrid dynasty that built the Alhambra, was the last Muslim state. It surrendered to Ferdinand and Isabella in January 1492.

Afterwards, Jews were ordered to convert or leave in 1492. Muslims were later forced to convert, and their descendants, the Moriscos, were expelled between 1609 and 1614.

## Key points

- Al-Andalus lasted from 711 to 1492.
- Córdoba was a major centre of science, medicine and philosophy.
- Historians debate how peaceful life was between faiths.
- Granada fell in 1492, the end of Muslim rule in Spain.

Further reading: Encyclopaedia Britannica, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

quiz.q: Where does the name Gibraltar come from?
options: Jabal Tariq, the mountain of Tariq
quiz.explain: Gibraltar comes from Jabal Tariq, named after Tariq ibn Ziyad.

quiz.q: Which city was the capital of the Umayyad state in Spain?
quiz.explain: Abd al-Rahman I made Córdoba the capital.

quiz.q: When did Granada surrender?
quiz.explain: Granada surrendered to Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492.

articles.title: World War I Explained Simply: Why It Started and What It Changed
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
World War I (1914 to 1918) shaped the world we live in, including many of the borders of the modern Middle East. Understanding it helps explain news stories that still matter today.

## How it started

By 1914, Europe's big powers were split into two groups that had promised to defend each other. Many historians list four deep causes: militarism (a race to build big armies), alliances, imperialism (competition for colonies) and nationalism (strong pride in one's nation).

The spark came on 28 June 1914. In Sarajevo, a young Bosnian Serb shot dead Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. Because of the alliances, Russia, Germany, France and Britain were pulled in within weeks.

## The two sides

- The Allies: mainly France, Britain, Russia, and later Italy (1915) and the United States (1917), plus many others.
- The Central Powers: Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria.

Soldiers came from all over the world, including India, Africa and Australia, because of the empires.

## A new kind of war

In western Europe, armies dug long lines of trenches (deep ditches). Machine guns, heavy guns and poison gas made attacks very deadly, and the lines hardly moved for years. Estimates of the dead vary, but about 15 to 20 million soldiers and civilians died.

In the Middle East, the Ottoman Empire fought the Allies at Gallipoli, in Mesopotamia (Iraq) and in Palestine. In 1916 the Arab Revolt began, led by Sharif Hussein of Mecca, with British support, against Ottoman rule.

## How it ended and what changed

Russia left the war after its 1917 revolution. With fresh American troops arriving, Germany asked for peace. The fighting stopped with an armistice (an agreement to stop fighting) on 11 November 1918.

The results were huge:

- Four empires collapsed: the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman.
- The Treaty of Versailles (1919) put heavy terms on Germany, which many historians link to the rise of World War II.
- Britain and France took control of much of the former Ottoman Middle East as "mandates". Arab leaders felt promises made during the war were broken, while British and French officials argued their deals were within the war's agreements. This debate continues among historians.
- The League of Nations was created to keep peace, an early form of the United Nations.

## Key points

- The war began after the killing of Archduke Franz Ferdinand on 28 June 1914.
- Alliances turned a local conflict into a world war.
- About 15 to 20 million people died.
- The Ottoman Empire collapsed, and new borders were drawn in the Middle East.

Further reading: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Imperial War Museums, National WWI Museum and Memorial

quiz.q: What event sparked World War I?
options: The killing of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
quiz.explain: The war began after Franz Ferdinand was shot in Sarajevo in 1914.

quiz.q: Which side was the Ottoman Empire on?
quiz.explain: The Ottoman Empire fought with Germany as one of the Central Powers.

quiz.q: When did the fighting stop?
quiz.explain: The armistice was signed on 11 November 1918.

articles.title: The Fall of the Berlin Wall and the End of the Cold War
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
For nearly 30 years, a concrete wall split the city of Berlin in two. Its sudden fall in 1989 became a symbol of the end of the Cold War, a rivalry that shaped politics everywhere, including in the Middle East and Asia.

## What was the Cold War?

After World War II, the world's two strongest countries, the United States and the Soviet Union (USSR), became rivals. The US led a group of countries with market economies and elected governments. The USSR led a group of communist states, where one party ruled and the state controlled the economy. It was called "cold" because the two never fought each other directly, though they backed opposite sides in wars elsewhere, such as Korea, Vietnam and Afghanistan.

## Why was the wall built?

Germany was divided after 1945. West Germany was allied with the US; East Germany (the GDR) was allied with the USSR. Berlin, inside East Germany, was also split. Millions of East Germans moved to the West, many through Berlin. To stop this, East German authorities built a wall starting on 13 August 1961. They said it protected the country; Western governments saw it as a prison wall.

Many people tried to escape. Researchers count at least 140 people who were killed at the wall or died because of the border system between 1961 and 1989.

## How did it fall?

In the 1980s, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev started reforms and said he would not use force to hold East Europe. Protests grew in Poland, Hungary and East Germany. On 9 November 1989, an East German official announced new travel rules at a press conference and, by mistake, said they started immediately. Crowds rushed to the border. Guards opened the gates, and people began to break down the wall.

## What came after

- Germany reunified on 3 October 1990.
- Communist governments across Eastern Europe ended, mostly peacefully.
- The Soviet Union broke up in December 1991 into 15 independent countries, ending the Cold War.

Views differ on what caused the end. Some stress Western pressure, others Gorbachev's reforms, the weak Soviet economy, or the courage of ordinary citizens who protested peacefully. Most historians agree all played a part. Not everyone gained at once: many people in the former East lost jobs in the hard years after.

## Key points

- The Cold War was a rivalry between the US and the Soviet Union after 1945.
- The Berlin Wall was built in 1961 to stop East Germans leaving.
- It opened on 9 November 1989 after a confused announcement.
- Germany reunified in 1990, and the USSR ended in 1991.

Further reading: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Berlin Wall Foundation, Chronik der Mauer

quiz.explain: Crowds crossed after the border opened on 9 November 1989.

articles.title: Apollo 11: The First Humans on the Moon, 1969
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
On 20 July 1969, hundreds of millions of people watched on television as humans walked on the Moon for the first time. It remains one of the greatest achievements of science and engineering, and a good example of what careful teamwork can do.

## The space race

The Moon landing came out of the Cold War rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union. The Soviets launched the first satellite, Sputnik, in 1957 and sent the first human into space, Yuri Gagarin, in 1961. In 1961, US President John F. Kennedy set a goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the end of the decade.

## The mission

Apollo 11 launched from Florida on 16 July 1969 on a huge Saturn V rocket. It had three astronauts:

- Neil Armstrong, the commander.
- Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin, the lunar module pilot.
- Michael Collins, who stayed in orbit around the Moon in the command module.

On 20 July, Armstrong and Aldrin landed in the lunar module, called Eagle, in an area named the Sea of Tranquility. Fuel was running low, and Armstrong had to steer past a field of rocks by hand. He then radioed: "The Eagle has landed."

Hours later, Armstrong stepped onto the surface and said: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." The two men spent about two and a half hours walking outside. They set up science experiments, took photos and collected about 21.5 kilograms of Moon rock and soil.

The crew returned safely to Earth, landing in the Pacific Ocean on 24 July 1969.

## What it achieved

- Scientists still study the Moon samples today. They helped show the Moon probably formed from material thrown out when a large object hit the early Earth.
- In total, NASA landed six Apollo missions, and 12 astronauts walked on the Moon. The last was Apollo 17 in December 1972.
- The programme pushed forward computers, materials and engineering.

There were costs and debates too. Apollo was very expensive, and some people at the time argued the money should have gone to problems on Earth. The programme also had tragedy: three astronauts died in a fire during a test for Apollo 1 in 1967.

## Why it still matters

Space agencies, including NASA with its Artemis programme, plan to send people back to the Moon. Today many countries, including the UAE, Saudi Arabia, India and China, have space programmes.

## Key points

- Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969.
- Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the surface; Michael Collins stayed in orbit.
- Six missions landed, and 12 people have walked on the Moon.
- The landing grew out of the Cold War space race.

Further reading: NASA, Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, Encyclopaedia Britannica

quiz.explain: Michael Collins stayed in orbit in the command module.

quiz.explain: Six Apollo missions landed, and 12 astronauts walked on the Moon.

quiz.explain: It grew out of the US-Soviet space race.

articles.title: From Pearls to Oil: How Oil Changed the Gulf
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
In less than one lifetime, many Gulf towns changed from small fishing and pearling ports into modern cities. The main reason was oil. Knowing this history helps explain why Gulf countries are now working hard to build economies that do not depend on oil alone.

## Life before oil

Before the 1930s, many Gulf economies depended on pearl diving, fishing, trade and date farming. Pearl diving was hard and dangerous work. In the 1930s, the pearl trade collapsed. Two reasons are usually given: cheaper cultured pearls (pearls grown on farms) from Japan, and the world economic crisis called the Great Depression.

## The big discoveries

Oil was first found in the wider region in Persia (Iran) in 1908. Then came a series of finds on the Arab side of the Gulf:

1. 1932: Bahrain, the first oil discovery on the Arab side of the Gulf.
2. 1938: Kuwait, at the giant Burgan field.
3. March 1938: Saudi Arabia, when the well called Dammam No. 7 struck oil in commercial amounts after years of failed drilling.
4. 1939: Qatar, at Dukhan.
5. 1958 to 1960: Abu Dhabi, first offshore at Umm Shaif and then on land. Its first oil export left Das Island in 1962.
6. 1964: Oman, with exports starting in 1967.

World War II slowed production, so the big growth came after 1945.

## Who controlled the oil?

At first, foreign oil companies from Britain and the United States held most of the rights and took much of the profit. Over time, producing countries won a bigger share. In 1960, at a meeting in Baghdad, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela founded OPEC, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, to coordinate their oil policies. During the 1970s, many Gulf states took full or majority ownership of their oil industries. For example, Saudi Arabia took full ownership of Aramco by 1980.

## How life changed

- Governments built schools, hospitals, roads, airports and water desalination plants.
- Many citizens moved to cities, and large numbers of foreign workers arrived.
- Gulf states became important in world politics because the world needed their energy.

There were challenges as well. When oil prices fall, government budgets suffer. Economists call heavy reliance on one product a risk. This is why plans like Saudi Vision 2030 and similar plans in other Gulf states aim to grow tourism, technology, industry and other sectors.

## Key points

- Before oil, many Gulf economies relied on pearling, fishing and trade.
- Bahrain found oil in 1932, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia in 1938, Qatar in 1939.
- OPEC was founded in 1960 in Baghdad.
- Gulf states now aim to diversify, so their economies depend less on oil.

Further reading: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Saudi Aramco, The National (UAE)

quiz.explain: Bahrain found oil in 1932, the first on the Arab side.

quiz.explain: Dammam No. 7 struck oil in commercial amounts in 1938.

options: Relying on oil is risky when prices fall
quiz.explain: Falling oil prices hurt budgets, so they are growing other sectors.

articles.title: US widens Iran blockade to land routes as Tehran drops missile range limit
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
On 7 November 2026, the US military said it had set up a new team to stop Iran moving weapons and banned goods over land and across the Caspian Sea. On the same day, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Iran would no longer keep its own 2,000-kilometre limit on the range of its missiles.

## What is Task Force Iron Gate?

US Central Command (CENTCOM) runs US forces in the Middle East. Its commander, Admiral Brad Cooper, ordered the new unit, called Task Force Iron Gate. It has about 20 military and civilian staff and is based in Tampa, Florida, in the United States. It will work with other US government agencies.

The US already has a naval blockade of Iran's ports. A blockade means ships are stopped from going in or out. The new team aims to block other routes, such as land borders and the Caspian Sea, which lies between Iran, Russia and three other countries. Cooper said it would limit Iran's ability to "finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military."

CENTCOM did not say how the team will stop these shipments, or whether it will work with Iran's neighbours. CENTCOM also says the sea blockade has stopped Iran from exporting more than $25 billion of crude oil. This figure has not been checked independently. Iraq's foreign minister, Fuad Hussein, said the US had asked Iraq to close all but two of its border crossings with Iran. He did not say if Iraq agreed.

An Iranian Revolutionary Guards spokesman called the plan "just a play on words."

## Iran's missile warning

Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said the old 2,000 km limit no longer applies. He did not say if Iran has working missiles that can fly further. Iranian leaders warned that any new attack would get a reply "without geographical restrictions."

## Ships hit near Hormuz

The sea around Oman and the Strait of Hormuz stayed dangerous this week:

- On 7 November, US forces disabled a cargo ship, the M/V Huda, in the Gulf of Oman. CENTCOM said its crew tried to break the blockade.
- A tanker caught fire near Khasab in Oman. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said its crew was evacuated.
- Iran's Revolutionary Guards said tankers hit mines while using "unauthorised" routes. These claims have not been confirmed.
- The UAE coast guard rescued 22 crew from a burning cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman. All were reported stable.

Talks also continue. Qatar is helping with diplomacy, and the Saudi and Qatari foreign ministers spoke by phone about calming tensions.

Sources: Gulf News, Stars and Stripes, Iran International

articles.title: South Africa's ANC has its worst local election result since 1994
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
South Africa's ruling party, the African National Congress (ANC), had its worst result in local elections since the end of apartheid in 1994. The vote for city and town councils was held on 4 November 2026, and almost all votes had been counted by 8 November.

## The results

With 99% of votes counted:

- The ANC, the party of President Cyril Ramaphosa, won about 31%. That is about 14 percentage points lower than in the 2021 local elections. South African media put its share at 30.81%.
- The Democratic Alliance (DA), the main rival, won about 25%.
- The MK party of former President Jacob Zuma came third with about 10%.
- Hundreds of smaller parties shared the rest.

The ANC is still the largest party. But it did not win a majority in any of the eight biggest cities, called metros, including Johannesburg and Pretoria. In Johannesburg, the country's biggest city, the DA had about 35% and the ANC about 20%. A higher share of voters took part than in 2021. Local media put turnout at around 52% to 54%, compared with about 46% last time.

## Why voters turned away

Many voters are angry about corruption, high unemployment, which is above 34%, and frequent problems with water and electricity supplies. Local councils are in charge of many of these daily services.

## What the parties say

ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula called the result "catastrophic." He said the party would not beg for positions and must "go home and put our house in order."

The DA said it will talk to parties that share its aim of "clean and accountable government." Its Johannesburg candidate, Helen Zille, could become mayor, depending on coalition deals.

## What happens next

Parties now have 14 days to make deals before the new councils meet. In many cities no party has more than half the seats, so they must form coalitions, which are groups of parties that agree to govern together.

The ANC and the DA already share power in the national government since 2024. They must now decide whether to work together in the cities or with smaller parties. One analyst said a poor outcome could lead to calls for Ramaphosa to step down early, but there has been no official move to do this.

Sources: Al Jazeera, IOL, The Citizen, CNBC Africa

articles.title: Qatar gets ready to host 48 teams at the U-17 World Cup from November 19
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Qatar will host the FIFA U-17 World Cup from November 19 to December 13, 2026. The tournament is for national teams of players aged 17 and under, and 48 teams will take part.

FIFA is the world governing body of football. This is the second year in a row that Qatar hosts the event. Qatar has the rights to host five editions in a row, up to 2029.

## How the tournament works

- 48 teams are split into 12 groups of four.
- The top two teams in each group, plus the eight best third-placed teams, go through to a round of 32.
- All matches are played at the Aspire Zone sports complex in Doha, the capital. Teams, fans and scouts stay close together, which organisers call a centralised model.
- There are eight matches a day during the group stage and the round of 32.
- On most days the first matches start at 3:30 pm local time. On Thursdays and Fridays they start at 4:00 pm.
- The final is on December 13. Reports differ on the stadium: Gulf Times named Khalifa International Stadium, but a related report named Ahmad bin Ali Stadium.

## The groups

The draw was held in Zurich, Switzerland, on May 21, 2026. Some of the groups:

- Group A: Qatar, Egypt, Panama and Greece. The Qatar Football Association highlighted the match between Qatar and Egypt.
- Group D: France, Uruguay, Saudi Arabia and Haiti, according to Saudi newspaper Okaz and other reports.
- Group G: Belgium, Mali, New Zealand and Vietnam.
- Group H includes Spain and Morocco.
- Group L includes Japan and Colombia, the champions of Asia and South America at this age level.

Five countries are playing in the tournament for the first time: Montenegro, Greece, Romania, Serbia and Vietnam. Arab teams taking part include Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Morocco.

## Last year's event

The 2025 edition was the first with 48 teams. According to Gulf Times, it involved 1,008 players and 104 matches on eight pitches. It drew more than 197,000 fans, and around 130 scouts from top clubs came to watch young players.

Sources: Qatar Football Association, Gulf Times, Qatar News Agency, Okaz, VietNamNet

articles.title: Houthi Missiles Hit Saudi Cities: From Riyadh Airport to an Aramco Tower
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
On November 8, 2026, Saudi Arabia said it shot down missiles fired at Riyadh and the Eastern Province. Falling debris damaged an office building of Saudi Aramco, the state oil company, in Riyadh. No one was reported hurt.

The missiles came from the Houthis, an armed group from Yemen that is supported by Iran and controls Yemen's capital, Sanaa. The Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia many times since a truce in Yemen's war collapsed in July 2026.

## What happened on November 8

Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy called it an "attempted" attack. State media said the Aramco building was hit by "falling shrapnel". Several news agencies said the damaged building was an Aramco tower in the King Abdullah Financial District, Riyadh's business area.

Major-General Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said two missiles were aimed at Riyadh and one at the Eastern Province. The coalition said it also stopped two missiles over the south of the kingdom and one drone.

## The deadliest attack: Riyadh airport

The worst attack so far happened on October 10, 2026, at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Saudi authorities said 12 people were killed and more than 300 were injured. The civil aviation authority gave a figure of 309 injured. Later, the Associated Press reported that an injured Indian citizen had died, which would bring the total to 13.

- Saudi authorities said the dead were four Saudis and eight foreigners.
- Two days earlier, three people, including an airline pilot, were killed in attacks on the same airport.
- On October 11, the airport was hit again. Reports said one person was killed and 11 were injured.

Reports described the October 10 attack as the deadliest in the kingdom since a suicide bombing in 2015.

## Other targets

According to Al Jazeera, the Houthis have also targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, the Ras Tanura and Rabigh oil refineries, other airports and Aramco sites. In late October, Reuters reported that Aramco told staff to leave its headquarters in Dhahran.

## The war inside Yemen

Fighting continues inside Yemen too. On November 7, a Houthi health official said coalition air strikes near Sanaa killed 33 people, including 13 children. The coalition did not comment, and Al Jazeera could not confirm the report. The UN says more than 1,600 people have been killed and almost 300,000 forced from their homes since the truce collapsed.

Sources: Al Jazeera, Reuters, Associated Press, Euronews

articles.title: COP31 Climate Summit Opens in Türkiye With Money and Fossil Fuels in Focus
articles.body:
The United Nations climate summit COP31 opens on Monday, November 9, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, and runs until November 20. Countries will discuss money for poorer nations, the move away from fossil fuels, and how to protect people from a warming world.

## An unusual double leadership

"COP" means "Conference of the Parties", the yearly meeting of countries in the UN climate treaty. Both Türkiye and Australia wanted to host COP31, so they agreed to share. Türkiye hosts the event and runs its "Action Agenda" of voluntary projects. Türkiye's environment minister, Murat Kurum, is the COP31 president. Australia's climate minister, Chris Bowen, leads the formal negotiations.

World leaders will speak on November 11 and 12. Türkiye says 91 heads of state and government have confirmed they will attend. Brazil's Lula, the UK's Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Spain's Pedro Sánchez are among the named speakers. China and India are not sending their top leaders. One briefing said the US government under President Trump is not taking part in the negotiations.

## The main issues

- Money: This is expected to be the hardest topic. At COP30 in Brazil last year, countries agreed to at least triple money for adaptation (protecting people from climate impacts) by 2035, but did not say how. A UN report says even that would cover less than a third of what developing countries need. The EU is reported to be arriving with no new money.
- Fossil fuels: Brazil has published a voluntary roadmap for moving away from oil, gas and coal, with steps up to 2033. Oil and gas producing countries oppose mentioning it in the final decision. Europe and small island nations may push for it.
- Just transition: A new system to help workers and communities during the energy shift is expected to be a main result, but countries disagree about what it should cover.
- Trade: China wants to discuss trade rules that limit clean technology, such as European carbon border taxes. African countries also asked for trade and adaptation money to be added to the agenda.

Türkiye also wants countries to raise electricity's share of energy use to 35% by 2035, and it is preparing an ocean declaration.

## The science

Scientists now say it is almost certain that the world will pass 1.5°C of warming above pre-industrial levels, the safer limit in the Paris Agreement. The UN's most hopeful scenario sees warming peak at about 1.7 to 1.8°C around the middle of the century before falling.

The summit begins as a very strong El Niño weather pattern brings new risks of drought, floods and hunger in many parts of the world.

Sources: Climate Home News, Carbon Brief, Council on Foreign Relations, Anadolu Agency, Türkiye Today

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is due on November 19 after years of waiting
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI), one of the most expected video games ever, is scheduled for release on November 19, 2026. The game is made by Rockstar Games, which is owned by the US company Take-Two Interactive. Take-Two will report its latest financial results on November 9, ten days before the launch.

## Release details

According to Take-Two and published guides:

- Platforms: PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S
- Price in the US: $79.99 for the Standard Edition and $99.99 for the Ultimate Edition
- Pre-orders opened on June 25, 2026
- Players with digital copies can download ("pre-load") the game from November 12

Rockstar has not announced a version for PC computers. Earlier GTA games also came to PC later than to consoles.

The game is set in a fictional version of Florida called Leonida, including the city of Vice City. It follows two main characters, Jason and Lucia.

## Two delays

The game was first expected in 2025. It was then moved to May 26, 2026, and later delayed again to November 19, 2026. Take-Two's chief executive, Strauss Zelnick, said in May that the company had an "exceptional start to preorders". He did not share sales numbers.

GTA V, the previous game in the series, came out in 2013 and became one of the best-selling games of all time. This is one reason why investors are watching GTA VI closely.

## Pressure on Take-Two

Take-Two expects net bookings (a measure of sales) of $8.0 billion to $8.2 billion in its financial year ending in March 2027. Most of this depends on GTA VI. Even so, Take-Two's share price has fallen more than 20% this year, according to Benzinga in October.

The company has also faced leaks. Videos said to show gameplay appeared online in August 2026. In October, a group calling itself "CYBERLEEK" threatened to leak the full game. It is not clear if it can do this. Some online posts have claimed another delay to 2027, but there is no official confirmation of this. Take-Two and Rockstar still list November 19 as the release date.

The launch is also important for Sony and Microsoft, whose consoles have become more expensive in 2026 because of rising memory chip prices.

Sources: Take-Two Interactive, Consequence, Variety, Benzinga, Notebookcheck

articles.title: Israel's president asks Eisenkot, not Netanyahu, to form a government
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
On 7 November 2026, Israel's President Isaac Herzog chose Gadi Eisenkot to try to form the country's next government, instead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It follows an election on 27 October in which no group won a majority.

## The election result

Israel's parliament, the Knesset, has 120 seats. A government needs the support of at least 61.

- Netanyahu's right-wing and religious group of parties won 53 seats.
- The group of parties led by Eisenkot won 48 seats.
- Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats.

Eisenkot is a former head of Israel's army, from 2015 to 2019. He now leads a party called Yashar. Palestinian citizens of Israel voted in record numbers, according to NBC News.

## Fraud claims rejected

Netanyahu's side made claims of fraud and foreign interference. On 4 November, the Central Elections Committee confirmed the results. Its acting head said there was "no basis" for claims of large-scale problems. Netanyahu has continued to challenge the outcome. Qatar denied claims by his allies that it interfered.

## Why Herzog chose Eisenkot

After the vote, the president asks party leaders who they support. Eisenkot was backed by 67 members of parliament, including Arab-led parties. Netanyahu had 46.

Eisenkot has 28 days to build a coalition, which is a group of parties that agree to govern together. He can get 14 more days if needed. If he fails, another person can try. If no government is formed, a new election must be held within 90 days, and Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister until then.

## A hard path to 61 seats

Eisenkot has said he will not bring Arab-led parties into his government. If he wins the support of the two ultra-Orthodox religious parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, he would have exactly 61 seats. He could also lead a smaller government if it wins a vote of confidence in parliament.

Ahmad Tibi of the Arab-led Joint List said he expects a minority government with outside support from Arab parties. Netanyahu warned that such a government would harm Israel.

Sources: Al Jazeera, NBC News, CNN

articles.title: France sees fourth weekend of protests over living costs
articles.body:
Large crowds marched across France on Saturday, 7 November 2026, the fourth weekend in a row of protests over the cost of living and public services. Police and protesters clashed in Paris and several other cities.

## How big were the protests?

The numbers depend on who is counting:

- France's Interior Ministry said 146,000 people marched nationwide, including 46,000 in Paris.
- A group of youth unions said 250,000 people marched, including 75,000 in Paris.
- At least 360 people were arrested across the country, according to a ministry count reported by the AFP news agency.

Turnout was lower than on the three weekends before. Two days earlier, on 5 November, a general strike backed by trade unions drew 575,000 people nationwide, according to the ministry.

In Paris, police used tear gas on people throwing objects at the end of the march. Rubbish bins were set on fire in several cities. Police blocked a banned gathering of the Yellow Vests, a protest movement that began in 2018 over fuel taxes, and arrested two of its leaders.

## How did it start?

The protests began in late September with high-school students. They complained about missing teachers, crowded classes, old school buildings and stress over Parcoursup, the national website used to apply to university. University students and trade unions later joined, and the movement grew into wider anger about prices. Reports say diesel prices rose sharply this autumn because of shipping blockades in the Middle East.

The unrest has at times been violent. In October, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said about 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers and gendarmes injured in one round of protests. Human rights groups, including Amnesty International, criticised the police for using strong crowd-control weapons that injured young people.

## Budget trouble and a moved meeting

The protests come at a hard time for the government. On 5 November, members of parliament rejected the tax and revenue part of the 2027 budget. The government's original plan now goes to the Senate, the upper house of parliament, which starts its debate on 20 November.

Lecornu is due to meet trade unions and employers on Monday, 9 November, to talk about wages and buying power.

The unrest has also affected diplomacy. France moved a meeting of G7 foreign ministers from Marseille to Paris at the last minute. The G7 is a group of seven large economies. The foreign ministry said the change was for practical reasons, but Reuters linked it to the weeks of protests. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is due in Paris from 8 to 10 November for the talks.

Sources: CNBC, Reuters, AFP, Al Jazeera

articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.title: Colombia hit by deadly drone and truck bomb attacks
articles.body:
Colombia saw a series of deadly attacks on its armed forces in the first week of November 2026. On Saturday, 7 November, drones carrying explosives hit an army base in the town of Santa Rosa del Sur, killing three soldiers. Six days earlier, a truck bomb in the town of Planadas killed four civilians, including a baby.

## The drone attack in Santa Rosa del Sur

Santa Rosa del Sur is in the south of Bolivar department, in northern Colombia. It is a gold-mining area where several armed groups fight for control.

- The army said the drones had been changed to carry explosives and struck buildings at the base around midday.
- The army and the president's office said three soldiers were killed and eight wounded. The AP news agency later reported at least 16 people injured, and one local outlet gave a higher number. The final figure is not yet clear.
- No group has claimed the attack. Early reports pointed to the possible involvement of the ELN (National Liberation Army), a left-wing guerrilla group active in the area, but this is not confirmed.

## The truck bomb in Planadas

On the night of Sunday, 1 November, attackers set off a dump truck packed with explosives near an army battalion in Planadas, in Tolima department in southern Colombia. Four civilians were killed, including a two-month-old baby, and 17 people were injured, according to UPI. Homes were destroyed and a curfew was ordered in the town.

Tolima's governor, Adriana Magali Matiz, called it a "vile and criminal act." Regional authorities named a group called the Ismael Ruiz Front as the main suspect. It is a faction of dissidents from the FARC, the rebel group that signed a peace deal with the government in 2016. Dissidents are fighters who rejected that deal. Formal blame has not yet been confirmed.

In a third attack, on 31 October and 1 November, explosive drones killed two soldiers and wounded five in Choco department. The army blamed the ELN.

## A growing threat

Cheap drones that drop explosives have become a major weapon for armed groups in Colombia. According to a Reuters report from January 2026, Colombia recorded 264 drone attacks in 2024 and 2025, killing 15 soldiers and wounding 153.

The armed groups fight over land, drug trafficking routes, illegal mining and extortion. The government has sent extra troops to Planadas and is investigating the attacks.

Sources: Saudi Gazette, UPI, AP, Colombia One, The Rio Times

articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.title: Pakistani astronaut to be first foreign visitor to China's space station
articles.body:
China said on Saturday, November 7, 2026, that an astronaut from Pakistan will fly on its next crewed mission, Shenzhou-24. The person will be the first foreign national to visit Tiangong, China's space station in orbit around Earth.

## What was announced

Chinese space officials said the Pakistani astronaut will fly as a "payload specialist". This is a crew member whose main job is to carry out scientific experiments, not to fly the spacecraft.

- The astronaut will make a short trip to the station.
- They will return to Earth on the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, which has been docked at Tiangong since May 2026.
- China did not say who was chosen.
- China did not give a launch date, but reports say the flight is expected before the end of 2026.

In October, Pakistan's Federal Minister for Planning, Ahsan Iqbal, said the mission would take place on November 25. China has not confirmed this date.

## Who could fly

In April 2026, two Pakistani candidates, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud, were selected to train in China. Both have trained at China's astronaut centre in Beijing. Reports say one will fly and the other will stay ready as a backup. Pakistan's Prime Minister, Shehbaz Sharif, met the two candidates in April and called the mission a "matter of pride for the entire nation".

## How it came about

The plan began with an agreement in February 2025 between China's human spaceflight agency, the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA), and Pakistan's space agency, known as SUPARCO. Under the deal, Pakistani candidates would train in China for a flight to Tiangong.

This will be Pakistan's first part in a human spaceflight. It is also a first for Tiangong, which until now has only hosted Chinese astronauts.

## About Tiangong

Tiangong means "Heavenly Palace" in Chinese. China built the station itself and usually keeps a crew of three people on board. Crews travel there on Shenzhou spacecraft, launched on Long March rockets from the Jiuquan launch centre in northwest China. China has said it is open to hosting astronauts from other countries, and this mission would be the first time that happens.

Some details, such as the exact length of the visit, have not been officially confirmed. Some reports describe it as about one week.

Sources: Pakistan Today, China in Space, Wikipedia (Shenzhou 24)

articles.title: US Midterms: Democrats Win Control of Both the House and the Senate
articles.body:
Americans voted in the midterm elections on November 3, 2026. The Democratic Party is projected to win control of both parts of Congress: the House of Representatives and the Senate. This is a big defeat for President Donald Trump's Republican Party.

## What are the midterms?

The midterms happen in the middle of a president's four-year term. This year, voters chose all 435 members of the House and 35 of the 100 senators. Congress makes laws and controls government spending, so the result will change how much power President Trump has for the next two years.

## The results so far

Counting is not finished, so the final numbers can still change.

- Senate: CBS News projects Democrats will have at least 54 seats when the new Congress starts in January. Democrats took seats from Republicans in Texas, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Maine.
- House: NBC News counted 252 seats for Democrats and 162 for Republicans on Friday, November 6, with 21 races not yet decided. A party needs 218 seats for a majority.
- Still too close to call: Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom led Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 2,500 votes on November 6, with mail ballots still being counted.

Some winners are well known. Former Ohio senator Sherrod Brown and former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper won Senate seats. In Texas, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed won a Democratic seat; he would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate. In Maine, long-serving Republican Senator Susan Collins lost to Troy Jackson.

## Why did voters choose this?

Exit polls (surveys of people after they vote) showed that most voters in close Senate states did not approve of President Trump's work. Many said their money situation was worse than before. Candidates and observers pointed to high living costs, tariffs (taxes on imports) and the war with Iran as problems for Republicans.

## What happens next

The new Congress begins in January 2027. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said "Americans are calling for accountability, not accommodation." He promised to "entangle" Trump "in legislative razor wire" if the president breaks the law. Republican Senate leader John Thune spoke with Trump after the results and is expected to keep his leadership role.

With control of both chambers, Democrats will be able to block laws the president wants and to open investigations into his government. Leaders abroad are also watching: Japan's prime minister said she will keep working with President Trump, and Ukraine's president said he hopes the new Congress will give Ukraine stronger support.

Sources: CBS News, NBC News, Yahoo News, Kyiv Post, Nippon.com

articles.title: Ukraine: Short Local Truce Ends as New Peace Talks Set for Abu Dhabi
articles.body:
A small, local ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia allowed civilians to leave the occupied town of Oleshky from October 27 to November 1, 2026. Now Ukrainian, Russian and US officials are expected to hold new talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10.

## The Oleshky ceasefire

Oleshky is a town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region. Russian forces have controlled it since 2022. Residents asked for help to leave from early 2026.

The local ceasefire lasted almost six days. US First Lady Melania Trump helped to arrange it. She said nearly 800 people were evacuated during the humanitarian mission. Ukraine's human rights official, Dmytro Lubinets, led the Ukrainian side. He said more residents are now asking to leave. The Kremlin (Russia's government) has said it does not plan more operations like this for now.

## Zelensky: "It worked"

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Oleshky shows that a ceasefire can be agreed quickly. "The decision to establish a ceasefire in Oleshky was made very quickly. And it worked," he said. He said a wider ceasefire could be checked using drones. In his view, the real problem is that Russian President Vladimir Putin does not want to stop the war.

In a German TV interview published around November 6, Zelensky said he had asked the United States to arrange a winter ceasefire with Russia. This would protect Ukraine's energy system and could make a presidential election possible. He said voting during martial law (special wartime rules) would be unfair, because millions of Ukrainians live abroad or under Russian occupation, and many soldiers are at the front.

## Russia's position

Russia has rejected Western plans for a full ceasefire with no conditions. It still demands that Ukraine give up the Donbas region in the east. Russia has also said the situation on the battlefield will decide when peace talks begin.

## Talks in Abu Dhabi

The talks in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, were first expected in October, after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Ukraine and Russia. The Kremlin then declined to take part. According to the Kyiv Independent, Russia will now send Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov, and European countries, including France, will also take part.

## Attacks continue

The war goes on while diplomats prepare. On the night of November 7, Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the area around it. Ukraine's air force said it shot down only four. Zelensky said Ukraine badly needs more Patriot air defence missiles and that the United States is best placed to help.

Sources: Kyiv Independent, Kyiv Post, Ukrainska Pravda, Council on Foreign Relations

articles.title: Hackers tried to heat French blood storage rooms, but no blood was lost
articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.body:
Hackers attacked the cold storage systems of France's national blood service on the night of 2 November 2026. They changed temperature settings at three sites. The service says no blood products were damaged and patients were not affected.

## What happened

The Établissement français du sang (EFS) collects blood donations in France and supplies hospitals. It keeps blood plasma and samples in cold rooms, some at around minus 30 degrees Celsius.

According to EFS and news reports:

- The attackers got in through a company that supplies EFS with refrigeration equipment, not through EFS's own systems.
- They changed the computer controls for temperature and defrosting in cold rooms at three EFS sites.
- They set the temperature limits to very high levels. The French newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported a target of 110 degrees Celsius. EFS has not confirmed an exact figure.
- Alarm systems spotted the changes quickly, so staff could act before any damage.

Some French media named the supplier, but EFS has not confirmed the name.

## No harm to patients

EFS said no blood products or samples were lost. Staff took back control of the equipment or switched it off, and moved products to other sites as a precaution. The affected cold rooms held plasma for transfusions and plasma used to make medicines. Blood collection and delivery to hospitals continued as normal.

## Who did it?

No one has said they carried out the attack, and no arrests have been reported. EFS is working with ANSSI, France's national cybersecurity agency, and the Ministry of Health.

## Part of a wider pattern

About two weeks earlier, in October, hackers attacked refrigeration systems in several French supermarkets. They raised freezer temperatures from a distance and destroyed frozen and chilled food. Reports say there have been similar attacks on cooling systems in other parts of Europe, and EU agencies are discussing a joint response.

## Why it matters

Many machines, from fridges to factory equipment, are now controlled over the internet. This makes them easier to manage, but also gives hackers new ways to cause real physical damage. Experts often say that a company is only as safe as its suppliers, because attackers can enter through a weaker partner.

Sources: The Connexion, Associated Press, BleepingComputer

articles.title: Belgium's king rejects PM De Wever's resignation over budget row
articles.body:
Belgium's King Philippe refused to accept the resignation of Prime Minister Bart De Wever on Friday, 6 November 2026. Instead, the king told him to go back to talks with his coalition partners and agree a budget.

De Wever had offered to resign on Monday, 2 November, after the parties in his government failed to agree on a spending plan for 2027.

## What is the dispute about?

Belgium has a coalition government. This means several parties share power because no single party won a majority. De Wever's government is made up of five parties.

De Wever wants to find about 10 billion euros by 2029 to close a gap in the public finances. He has proposed spending cuts and a rise in VAT, a sales tax paid on most goods and services. But the parties do not agree on who should carry the cost:

- De Wever's Flemish nationalist party, N-VA, and the French-speaking liberal party MR want more limits on spending, including in healthcare.
- MR opposes the VAT increase.
- The socialist and centrist partners want more of the money to come from taxes on wealth.

## What did the king do?

In Belgium, the king formally appoints and accepts the resignation of governments. The Royal Palace said King Philippe had "put his decision on hold" and first spoke with the leaders of the five governing parties.

According to the palace, those leaders promised to finish the budget talks quickly and said their parties would make concessions, meaning they would give up some of their demands. The talks are restarting straight away.

De Wever must report back to the king on Monday, 16 November. One outlet described the timeline differently, as a 10-day extension, but most reports give the 16 November date.

## Why it matters

Belgium is home to the main institutions of the European Union and NATO. Like several other European countries, including France, it is under pressure to reduce its budget deficit, which is the gap between what a government spends and what it collects in taxes.

If the talks fail again, the king could accept the resignation. That could lead to a long period of political uncertainty.

For now, the coalition stays in place, and the next few days will show whether the five parties can find a deal.

Sources: Euronews, Macau Business (AFP), QNC News

articles.author: Digest Editors
articles.title: Paraguay's president removed over bank collapse; Alliana sworn in
articles.body:
Paraguay has a new president. On Friday, 6 November 2026, the Senate removed President Santiago Pena from office over his links to the collapse of a digital bank. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in the same day, and prosecutors ordered Pena to be placed under house arrest.

Paraguay is a landlocked country in South America, between Brazil, Argentina and Bolivia.

## The bank collapse

The crisis began on Tuesday, 3 November, when the central bank said Ueno, a digital bank, no longer met legal rules on solvency. This means it did not have enough money and assets to cover its loans and other business. The bank was taken over and its remaining assets were moved to other banks.

The impact was large:

- Ueno had about 3 million members, nearly two-thirds of the country's adults.
- Many clients suddenly lost access to their accounts and pension payments.
- It was the fifth-largest bank in Paraguay by deposits.
- About $355 million of state pension money had been invested in it, according to Al Jazeera.

Pena was named in 2023 as a shareholder of Ueno's parent company. He says he sold his shares in early 2025.

## Resignation refused, then impeachment

Pena tried to resign, saying it was needed "to preserve our democratic institutions." But Congress rejected his resignation. Reports say that if he had been allowed to resign, he would have kept the right of former presidents to become a senator for life, which gives legal protection from prosecution.

On Thursday, the lower house voted 78 to zero to impeach him, which means to formally charge him. On Friday, 44 of the 45 senators voted to remove him, with one abstaining. Pena did not attend and sent his lawyers. He said he would cooperate with the investigation.

Prosecutors are investigating possible crimes including fraud, breach of trust and misuse of funds. At least 27 people face criminal charges. An arrest warrant was also issued for the former head of the central bank, Carlos Carvallo, who resigned earlier in the week.

## Who is Pedro Alliana?

Alliana, 52, is a conservative from the Colorado Party, which has dominated Paraguayan politics since 1948. He was governor of Neembucu department and spent nearly ten years in the lower house of parliament, including three years as its speaker. He will serve until the current term ends in August 2028. Congress must now choose a new vice president.

Sources: Al Jazeera, Euronews, Reuters, AP
